questions.chapter: What ADHD Is And Is Not
questions.question_text: According to this chapter, what is attention?

options.A: The brain's ability to select some information for processing and set the rest aside
options.B: The brain's total capacity for thinking
options.C: A fixed trait that cannot be trained
options.D: The opposite of hyperactivity

questions.explanation: The chapter defines attention as the brain's mechanism for selecting some information for processing while setting the rest aside, using the spotlight-in-a-theater image. Option B confuses attention with general intelligence. Option C is wrong because the chapter treats attention skills as trainable. Option D wrongly treats attention and hyperactivity as opposites rather than separate traits.

questions.chapter: What ADHD Is And Is Not
questions.question_text: The formal definition of ADHD is built from which three trait words?

options.A: Anxiety, depression, and mood
options.B: Memory, focus, and speed
options.C: Inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity
options.D: Distraction, fatigue, and irritability

questions.explanation: The chapter states the DSM-5 definition of ADHD is assembled from inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity, each given a precise clinical meaning. The other options list traits or moods that are not the load-bearing words of the diagnosis, though some (like fatigue) can co-occur with ADHD.

questions.chapter: What ADHD Is And Is Not
questions.question_text: Under DSM-5 criteria, several symptoms of ADHD must be present before what age for the "early onset" requirement to be met?

options.A: Age 6
options.B: Age 12
options.C: Age 18
options.D: Age 21

questions.explanation: DSM-5 requires several symptoms to be present before age 12, which is why the chapter notes that a late diagnosis at 27 or 45 means the explanation is new, not the condition itself. Age 6 is too early and not the DSM-5 threshold; ages 18 and 21 are well past the required early-onset window.

questions.chapter: What ADHD Is And Is Not
questions.question_text: What does classifying ADHD as a "neurodevelopmental disorder" mean?

options.A: It is caused by poor parenting during early childhood
options.B: It is a personality disorder that develops in adulthood
options.C: It only affects children and resolves by adolescence
options.D: It arises from differences in brain development, is present from childhood, and affects functioning across the lifespan

questions.explanation: The chapter defines a neurodevelopmental disorder as one arising from differences in brain development, present from childhood, that shapes functioning over a person's whole life. Option A contradicts the chapter's point that parenting doesn't cause ADHD. Options B and C mischaracterize ADHD as adult-onset or as something children outgrow entirely.

questions.chapter: What ADHD Is And Is Not
questions.question_text: Which statement best captures the difference between "attention" and "attention regulation" as this chapter defines them?

options.A: Attention is the raw capacity to focus, while attention regulation is directing that capacity where a person intends, on purpose
options.B: Attention regulation refers to how much attention a person has in total, while attention refers to its quality
options.C: They are two different names for the identical concept
options.D: Attention regulation only applies to hyperactivity, not inattention

questions.explanation: The chapter distinguishes attention (the capacity to focus) from attention regulation (steering that capacity on purpose rather than wherever the environment pulls it) using the spotlight-and-operator image. Option B reverses the relationship. Option C ignores a distinction the chapter builds the whole book on. Option D is wrong because regulation applies to inattention as much as hyperactivity.

questions.chapter: What ADHD Is And Is Not
questions.question_text: Based on the chapter, why is the inattentive presentation of ADHD often diagnosed later than the hyperactive presentation, especially in girls?

options.A: Inattentive symptoms are less common in the general population
options.B: Inattentive ADHD only appears after puberty
options.C: Inattention is invisible and doesn't disrupt others the way hyperactivity does, so it draws less attention from teachers and parents
options.D: Doctors are not trained to recognize inattentive symptoms at all

questions.explanation: The chapter explains that inattention is invisible — it looks like an empty seat or a lost permission slip rather than disruptive behavior — so it doesn't trigger the same alarm hyperactivity does, using Elena and Marcus as the worked example. Option A is not supported by the text. Option B is false; onset is before age 12. Option D overstates the issue as a training gap rather than a visibility gap.

questions.chapter: What ADHD Is And Is Not
questions.question_text: What do twin studies show about the role of genetics in ADHD?

options.A: Genetics play almost no role; environment explains nearly all cases
options.B: A single "ADHD gene" has been identified that determines the condition
options.C: Genetics only matter for the hyperactive presentation, not the inattentive one
options.D: ADHD has a heritability of roughly 70-80 percent, similar to height, with hundreds of gene variants each contributing slightly

questions.explanation: Twin studies put ADHD's heritability at roughly 70-80 percent, comparable to height, with hundreds of common gene variants each nudging the odds slightly rather than one single gene. Option A understates the strong genetic evidence. Option B contradicts the chapter's explicit statement that no single gene exists. Option C is not supported; heritability applies across presentations.

questions.chapter: What ADHD Is And Is Not
questions.question_text: What is the core flaw in the "willpower myth" — the idea that the fix for ADHD is simply trying harder?

options.A: People with ADHD have already tried harder for years before diagnosis, so more raw effort is a strategy that has already failed
options.B: Willpower doesn't exist as a psychological concept
options.C: Trying harder works for hyperactivity but not for inattention
options.D: The myth is correct, but only for children

questions.explanation: The chapter argues that by the time someone reaches an evaluation, they have usually spent years trying harder, so recommending more effort is prescribing a strategy already proven not to work — like willing yourself to see without glasses. Option B overstates the point; willpower exists but isn't the fix here. Options C and D invent exceptions the chapter never makes.

questions.chapter: What ADHD Is And Is Not
questions.question_text: Raj spends five hours absorbed in restoring an old motorcycle but can't make himself start a ten-minute insurance form due the same day. Using the "regulation lens" from this chapter, which explanation fits best?

options.A: Raj is lazy about paperwork but disciplined about hobbies
options.B: Raj's attention steers strongly toward interest and novelty and weakly toward flat, low-interest tasks, regardless of how much he wants to do them
options.C: Raj has more total attention for hobbies than for chores
options.D: Raj secretly doesn't care about the insurance deadline

questions.explanation: This mirrors the chapter's Maya example: attention steers toward interest and urgency and away from tedium, independent of how much the person genuinely wants to complete the task. Option A applies the laziness myth the chapter explicitly rejects. Option C misreads regulation as total capacity. Option D assumes indifference where the chapter argues the person usually cares and suffers over the undone task.

questions.chapter: What ADHD Is And Is Not
questions.question_text: A person suspects they have ADHD but delays seeking an evaluation because of jokes and dismissive comments they've heard about the diagnosis at work. According to the stigma cycle described in this chapter, what does this delay typically lead to next?

options.A: Faster diagnosis once symptoms become undeniable
options.B: No further effects, since stigma only affects public perception, not the individual
options.C: Years of unexplained struggle that get explained instead by myths like laziness or carelessness, which the person then internalizes as self-stigma
options.D: A reduction in symptom severity over time

questions.explanation: The chapter's stigma cycle traces how hiding and delaying evaluation leads to years of unexplained struggle, which gets explained by myths rather than facts, and those myth explanations are then internalized as self-stigma — illustrated by the teacher who waited three more years. Option A contradicts the chapter's teacher example. Options B and D ignore the compounding harm the chapter describes.

questions.question_text: What is executive function, as this chapter defines it?

options.A: The umbrella term for the mental skills that manage other skills, such as starting tasks, holding information in mind, and inhibiting impulses
options.B: A single brain region that controls movement
options.C: Another name for long-term memory
options.D: The medical term for hyperactivity

questions.explanation: Executive function is the umbrella name for the mental skills the prefrontal systems provide — skills that manage other skills, like starting a task, holding instructions in mind, and resisting distraction. Option B confuses it with a motor region. Option C is wrong because long-term memory is generally intact in ADHD and is a separate system. Option D mislabels a set of cognitive skills as a single symptom.

questions.question_text: According to this chapter, which brain region matures last, often not finishing until the mid-to-late twenties?

options.A: The visual cortex
options.B: The cerebellum
options.C: The default mode network
options.D: The prefrontal cortex

questions.explanation: The chapter explains that the prefrontal cortex — the region handling planning, self-control, and judgment — is the last major brain area to finish developing, running into the mid-to-late twenties. The visual cortex and movement-related regions mature much earlier. The default mode network is a functional network, not the late-maturing region itself.

questions.question_text: What is working memory, as described in this chapter?

options.A: The brain's permanent storage for facts and events
options.B: The small mental workspace that holds information while it's being used, such as an instruction while carrying it out
options.C: The system that controls physical balance
options.D: A synonym for long-term memory

questions.explanation: The chapter describes working memory as "the mental desk" — a small workspace that holds information while it is actively being used, illustrated by Priya losing instructions mid-errand. Options A and D describe long-term memory, a separate and generally intact system in ADHD. Option C describes an unrelated physical function.

questions.question_text: What is prospective memory?

options.A: Memory for facts learned in school
options.B: Memory for people's names
options.C: Memory for intentions — remembering to do something at the right future moment, without a prompt
options.D: Memory that improves with age

questions.explanation: Prospective memory is memory for intentions — remembering to act at the right moment, such as taking medication or picking up a prescription, with nothing external prompting the recall. Options A and B describe long-term memory for facts or names, a different system. Option D is not a claim the chapter makes.

questions.question_text: According to the chapter's discussion of delay aversion and the interest-based nervous system, what activates motivation most reliably in ADHD?

options.A: Interest, novelty, urgency, and challenge
options.B: Long-term importance and moral obligation
options.C: Careful step-by-step planning
options.D: Rewards that are distant but large

questions.explanation: The chapter describes the ADHD brain as running on an "interest-based nervous system," activated reliably by interest, novelty, challenge, and urgency, rather than by importance alone. Option B describes the importance-based activation that neurotypical planning relies on. Option C describes a planning skill, not a motivational trigger. Option D is contradicted by delay aversion, which makes distant rewards lose motivational pull fast.

questions.question_text: What does the chapter say happens to the default mode network during focused tasks in ADHD, and what is the consequence?

options.A: It shuts off completely and never activates
options.B: It only activates in people without ADHD
options.C: It has no connection to attention at all
options.D: It is suppressed less reliably during tasks, so daydreaming intrudes mid-task

questions.explanation: The chapter explains that the default mode network normally gets suppressed when focused work begins, but in ADHD that suppression is less reliable, so the mind wanders back into it mid-task — the "screensaver" flickering on. Options A and C misdescribe the network as inactive or irrelevant. Option B is false; everyone's default mode network activates during idle moments.

questions.question_text: Which statement correctly interprets the ADHD brain maturation lag finding?

options.A: It proves that any individual child with ADHD is exactly three years behind peers on a brain scan
options.B: It is a group-average finding showing delayed but similarly shaped cortical development, with some differences persisting into adulthood
options.C: It means ADHD is fully outgrown once the brain catches up around age 25
options.D: It shows brain scans can reliably diagnose ADHD in an individual

questions.explanation: The chapter is explicit that the maturation lag is a group-average research finding — cortical development follows the same route on a delayed timetable — and that some differences persist into adulthood, which is why ADHD is a lifespan condition. Option A over-applies a group statistic to an individual. Option C contradicts the chapter's point that the lag doesn't mean full catch-up. Option D is directly rejected: no scan can diagnose an individual.

questions.question_text: What is cognitive load, and why does the chapter emphasize it?

options.A: It is a measure of IQ that predicts ADHD severity
options.B: It is fixed and identical for everyone regardless of the day
options.C: It is the total demand on working memory and executive systems at a given moment, and it is invisible, so people get blamed for failures of a budget they've already overdrawn
options.D: It only affects people without ADHD

questions.explanation: Cognitive load is the total demand on working memory and executive systems at any moment, and the chapter stresses that because load is invisible, observers often blame a person for failures caused by an already-overdrawn budget, as in the dishwasher example. Option A confuses it with intelligence. Option B contradicts the chapter's point that load varies by time of day and prior demands. Option D is false; load affects everyone, just with a smaller and faster-draining budget in ADHD.

questions.question_text: Ben sits down at his desk wanting to start his tax return, but twenty minutes pass and he still hasn't opened the file, even though he understands exactly what to do. Which executive function does this scenario best illustrate failing?

options.A: Task initiation
options.B: Working memory
options.C: Cognitive flexibility
options.D: Self-monitoring

questions.explanation: This matches the chapter's description of task initiation as "the starter motor" — converting intention into the first action — where a person can want to start, know exactly what to do, and still be unable to launch. Working memory (B) concerns holding information in mind, not starting. Cognitive flexibility (C) concerns shifting between tasks or approaches. Self-monitoring (D) concerns tracking ongoing performance, not beginning it.

questions.question_text: Sam forgets to pick up his wife's prescription despite promising that morning; his wife concludes "if it mattered to him, he'd have remembered." Which option best analyzes what actually failed, according to the chapter?

options.A: Sam's long-term memory failed, since he couldn't recall the promise at all
options.B: Sam never truly formed the intention, so nothing failed
options.C: Sam's prospective memory failed — the intention was intact, but the brain's unprompted, self-firing alarm at the right moment didn't fire
options.D: Sam's working memory was overloaded at the moment he made the promise

questions.explanation: The chapter analyzes this exact example as a prospective memory failure: the intention was filed and genuine, but the unprompted, self-triggered alarm that should have fired at 5:15 didn't, which looks identical to not caring from the outside. Option A misidentifies the memory system involved. Option B contradicts the chapter's claim that Sam meant it completely. Option D misplaces the failure at the moment of promising rather than at the moment of action.

questions.question_text: According to the DSM-5, what are the three presentations of ADHD?

options.A: Mild, moderate, and severe
options.B: Childhood, adolescent, and adult
options.C: Predominantly inattentive, predominantly hyperactive-impulsive, and combined
options.D: Type A, Type B, and Type C

questions.explanation: The DSM-5 sorts ADHD into predominantly inattentive, predominantly hyperactive-impulsive, and combined presentations, based on which symptom category's threshold is met. Option A describes severity, not presentation. Option B describes ages, not diagnostic categories. Option D is a made-up labeling scheme not used in the DSM-5.

questions.question_text: What is time blindness?

options.A: A weakened felt sense of how much time has passed or how far away a deadline is
options.B: An inability to read a clock
options.C: A vision problem common in ADHD
options.D: Difficulty remembering past events

questions.explanation: Time blindness is a weakened felt sense of duration and deadlines, with the ADHD time horizon collapsed to "now" and "not now," illustrated by Dana believing getting ready always takes eight minutes. Option B confuses it with a literal reading skill. Option C misidentifies it as a vision issue. Option D describes long-term memory, a separate and generally intact system.

questions.question_text: What is masking, as this chapter defines it?

options.A: Wearing a literal face covering to reduce sensory input
options.B: A medication side effect
options.C: The formal diagnostic term for combined presentation
options.D: The continuous, effortful concealment of ADHD symptoms to appear fine

questions.explanation: Masking is the continuous, effortful concealment of symptoms — suppressing fidgeting, rehearsing sentences, arriving early to hide time blindness — illustrated by Grace, whose "organized" reputation was hand-built compensation. Option A is a literal misreading of the word. Option B misplaces it as a drug effect. Option C confuses it with an unrelated diagnostic category.

questions.question_text: What is hyperfocus?

options.A: Constant, low-grade distractibility
options.B: A state of intense, tunnel-vision absorption in which time and other signals are muted
options.C: The medical term for hyperactivity in adults
options.D: A symptom found only in the hyperactive-impulsive presentation

questions.explanation: Hyperfocus is described as intense, tunnel-vision absorption where hours vanish and hunger, bladder, and time signals are all muted — the same regulation coin's other face as distractibility. Option A describes the opposite pattern. Option C misnames an unrelated adult symptom. Option D is incorrect; hyperfocus appears across presentations, not just the hyperactive-impulsive one.

questions.question_text: Why can a child who can't sit through five minutes of homework manage to play chess or a video game for an hour, according to this chapter?

options.A: The child is choosing to misbehave only during homework
options.B: Chess and video games require no attention at all
options.C: Situational variability: interest, novelty, immediate feedback, and challenge raise motivation and lower load, so symptoms genuinely shrink in situations that supply them
options.D: The child has fully outgrown ADHD during enjoyable activities

questions.explanation: Situational variability explains that symptoms genuinely change strength with the situation, because interest, novelty, and immediate feedback raise the reward system's pull and lower cognitive load. Option A frames a mechanism as a choice. Option B is false; games demand real attention, just of a kind the brain readily supplies. Option D misreads a temporary situational effect as a permanent outcome.

questions.question_text: According to the chapter, why does masking contribute to ADHD being diagnosed late, especially in women?

options.A: Masking produces decent grades and performance, so nobody refers the person for evaluation, even though it is expensive to maintain
options.B: Masking makes symptoms disappear permanently
options.C: Masking is only possible for people without real ADHD
options.D: Masking is a treatment that cures the underlying condition

questions.explanation: The chapter explains masking works well enough to produce decent grades and reviews, so nobody refers the person for evaluation, even though maintaining the performance is expensive and eventually costly, as with Grace. Option B is false; masking conceals symptoms, it doesn't remove them. Option C contradicts the chapter's claim that masking is common precisely among people who do have ADHD. Option D confuses concealment with treatment.

questions.question_text: How does this chapter distinguish ADHD-related procrastination from ordinary laziness?

options.A: Procrastination in ADHD only happens with unimportant tasks
options.B: There is no meaningful difference; both describe the same thing
options.C: ADHD procrastination always resolves itself without a deadline
options.D: Procrastination in ADHD involves genuine suffering over the undone task and a failure of task initiation, not indifference to it

questions.explanation: The chapter describes ADHD procrastination as task initiation failure wearing a moral costume — the person suffers over the undone task, often doing decoy productivity, rather than feeling indifferent to it. Option A is unsupported; the tasks are often important. Option B collapses a distinction the chapter deliberately draws. Option C contradicts the chapter's point that urgency is usually what finally triggers action.

questions.question_text: Why does the chapter warn against treating someone's best-ever performance as their new normal?

options.A: Because people with ADHD deliberately perform worse on purpose after a good day
options.B: Because performance inconsistency means a great day reflects unusually aligned conditions, not a new sustainable baseline
options.C: Because good days are proof the person doesn't have ADHD
options.D: Because best-ever performances are always faked

questions.explanation: Performance inconsistency means a great performance reflects conditions lining up well that day, not a new floor the person can now be held to; treating it as the new minimum turns encouragement into an accusation. Option A wrongly implies intentional sabotage. Option C contradicts situational variability, which predicts inconsistency as a symptom, not its absence. Option D is an unsupported and uncharitable claim the chapter never makes.

questions.question_text: A father plans a completely unstructured, quiet Saturday for his wife with ADHD as a gift of rest, but by 10 am she has reorganized a closet and started laundry, visibly agitated by the stillness. Which trait from this chapter best explains her reaction?

options.A: Masking
options.B: Time blindness
options.C: Restlessness in adults, driven by discomfort with unstructured stillness
options.D: Decision paralysis

questions.explanation: This is the chapter's Priya example: restlessness in adults often looks like structural motion, and unstructured stillness produces under-arousal that the system escapes through activity. Masking (A) concerns concealing symptoms, not seeking motion. Time blindness (B) concerns duration perception, not restlessness. Decision paralysis (D) concerns freezing over choices, not filling stillness with action.

questions.question_text: Nora's son was diagnosed with combined presentation at age eight. At sixteen, he sits calmly through dinner, so Nora assumes he's "growing out of it," even as his grades quietly collapse from missed assignments. What does this chapter say is really happening?

options.A: His presentation has likely shifted toward inattentive as the visible motor moved inward, while the invisible half now drives the struggles
options.B: He no longer has ADHD, since the visible hyperactivity is gone
options.C: His calm at dinner proves the earlier diagnosis was incorrect
options.D: Grades dropping is unrelated to ADHD and points to a different cause entirely

questions.explanation: The chapter explains presentations are snapshots that shift with age — a hyperactive-impulsive child often becomes inattentive-looking as the visible motor goes inside, exactly as with Nora's son, whose collapsing grades signal the invisible half now running the show. Option B and C both mistake fading visible symptoms for the condition disappearing or never existing. Option D ignores the direct link the chapter draws between inattentive symptoms and missed assignments.

questions.question_text: What does the "gender diagnosis gap" describe?

options.A: Boys and girls receive ADHD diagnoses at nearly identical rates throughout life
options.B: Girls are diagnosed more often than boys at every age
options.C: Boys are diagnosed far more often than girls in childhood, but adult diagnosis rates approach parity
options.D: ADHD is diagnosed only in boys before puberty

questions.explanation: The gender diagnosis gap is the finding that boys are diagnosed roughly three-to-one over girls in childhood clinics, while adult diagnosis rates approach parity — evidence that girls carry the condition undetected rather than lacking it. Option A ignores this well-documented childhood disparity. Option B reverses the childhood pattern. Option D is false; ADHD occurs in girls before puberty too, just less often noticed.

questions.question_text: What is high achievement masking?

options.A: The mechanism by which intelligence, perfectionism, and social motivation build an industrial-grade compensation system that hides ADHD behind visible success
options.B: A medication that suppresses ADHD symptoms
options.C: A formal DSM-5 diagnostic specifier
options.D: The tendency of high achievers to never develop ADHD

questions.explanation: High achievement masking is the mechanism by which intelligence, perfectionism, and social motivation build a compensation system so effective that success itself hides the ADHD underneath, as with Sana's honor-roll transcript built on private all-nighters and panic. Option B misidentifies it as a drug. Option C misplaces it in the DSM-5, which has no such specifier. Option D contradicts the chapter's point that achievement can coexist with, and even conceal, ADHD.

questions.question_text: How does this chapter distinguish "reframing your past" from making excuses?

options.A: Reframing means blaming parents for causing the condition
options.B: There is no real difference; both avoid responsibility equally
options.C: Reframing only applies to people diagnosed in childhood
options.D: An excuse denies responsibility for the future; a reframe revises the explanation of the past while still owning future behavior

questions.explanation: The chapter draws a clear line: an excuse denies future responsibility, while a reframe revises how past events are explained without excusing anything going forward — the person still owns their behavior from here on. Option A contradicts Chapter 1's point that nobody causes ADHD. Option B collapses a distinction the chapter deliberately makes. Option C is false; reframing applies most often to adults diagnosed late.

questions.question_text: In the chapter's classroom example, why does Jonah get an evaluation by November while Amara, who has the same condition, does not?

options.A: Amara's family refuses to seek help
options.B: Referral runs on disruption: Jonah's behavior bothers others and gets noticed, while Amara's quiet inattention and strong reading skills trip no alarms
options.C: Amara doesn't actually have ADHD
options.D: Teachers are specifically trained to overlook girls

questions.explanation: The chapter explains that childhood referral runs on disruption — the child who bothers others gets flagged, while a quietly struggling child who reads ahead of grade level, like Amara, trips no alarms even with the same underlying condition. Option A is not stated or implied. Option C contradicts the chapter's premise that both children have ADHD. Option D overstates an unintentional pattern as deliberate training.

questions.question_text: Why does the chapter describe the transition to college as the "steepest cliff" in the academic sequence?

options.A: College classes are inherently more difficult academically than high school classes
options.B: College students no longer have access to any accommodations
options.C: College removes nearly all external scaffolding at once — parental schedules, teacher monitoring, daily deadlines — while demanding exactly the executive functions ADHD impairs
options.D: The transition to college happens with no warning, unlike earlier transitions

questions.explanation: The chapter emphasizes that college strips away parental schedules, teacher monitoring, and daily deadlines all at once, replacing them with demands on initiation, time management, and prospective memory — precisely the functions ADHD impairs. Option A misattributes the cliff to raw difficulty rather than lost scaffolding. Option B is false; accommodations exist in college, though a student must request them. Option D is inaccurate; the chapter notes the transition is foreseeable, which is why early preparation matters.

questions.question_text: Why does the chapter say relief and grief typically coexist after a late ADHD diagnosis, rather than one replacing the other?

options.A: Because grief is a symptom of ADHD itself
options.B: Because relief only applies to people diagnosed as children
options.C: Because most late-diagnosed adults regret being evaluated at all
options.D: Because the relief of finally having an explanation doesn't erase the real loss of decades spent misunderstanding oneself

questions.explanation: The chapter describes relief and grief as braided together: relief that there's finally a name and explanation, grief for the decades of self-blame and missed opportunities that a name might have prevented — both feelings are correct and don't cancel each other. Option A misclassifies grief as a symptom rather than an emotional response. Option B is false; the chapter applies this dynamic specifically to late diagnosis. Option C is contradicted by the chapter's overall case for the value of diagnosis.

questions.question_text: A 51-year-old woman who managed her ADHD symptoms well for decades suddenly finds herself unable to focus, blaming "menopause brain." Based on this chapter, what is the most accurate way to understand her situation?

options.A: Falling estrogen may be weakening the compensation systems that carried her for years, revealing a lifelong ADHD that masking had kept hidden — both hormonal and lifelong-history questions are worth asking
options.B: Her earlier ADHD must have been misdiagnosed, since real ADHD doesn't wait until 51 to appear
options.C: Menopause and ADHD are unrelated, so her focus problems must have a different cause entirely
options.D: She should assume this is normal aging and not worth investigating

questions.explanation: The chapter explains that falling estrogen at menopause weakens the compensation systems that had carried a woman for decades, so symptoms sharpen just as ADHD that was always there — but masked — finally becomes visible; both hormonal and lifelong-history questions are worth exploring together. Option B wrongly assumes symptoms can't have been present earlier under a mask. Option C contradicts the chapter's explicit hormone-ADHD connection. Option D dismisses a pattern the chapter treats as worth investigating.

questions.question_text: Sana's father realizes that her "careless" lost bus pass as a teenager was actually a working-memory failure, not a character flaw, and tells her so. Which best describes what he is doing?

options.A: Making an excuse for Sana's future behavior
options.B: Diagnosing Sana's ADHD, replacing the need for a professional evaluation
options.C: Reframing the past — revising his explanation of old events using the diagnosis, without excusing anything going forward
options.D: Blaming himself for causing her ADHD

questions.explanation: This is the chapter's closing example of reframing: the father revises how he explains past events, from character flaw to executive-function mechanism, without excusing anything about Sana's future conduct. Option A misapplies the excuse/reframe distinction the chapter draws. Option B overstates a parent's role; the professional evaluation already happened. Option D contradicts Chapter 1's settled point that parenting doesn't cause ADHD.

questions.question_text: A family wants to prepare their child with ADHD for the transition to college, following this chapter's advice. Which approach best fits the chapter's recommendation?

options.A: Wait until the student struggles in their first semester, then intervene
options.B: Have the student start running their own planner, medication, laundry, and wake-ups in eleventh grade, while a parent can still coach nearby and mistakes are cheap
options.C: Manage every detail of the student's schedule remotely once they leave for college
options.D: Assume college accommodations will automatically replace the need for any preparation

questions.explanation: The chapter recommends transferring systems before the transition, not after the crash — the student practicing self-management in eleventh grade while a parent can still coach from nearby and mistakes cost little. Option A is exactly the delayed approach the chapter warns against. Option C contradicts the chapter's point that remote control doesn't substitute for transferred skills. Option D wrongly assumes accommodations remove the need for the student's own executive habits.

questions.question_text: A colleague claims the rise in adult ADHD diagnoses is "obviously overdiagnosis driven by social media." Which response best reflects this chapter's analysis?

options.A: The rise partly reflects a real backlog of missed diagnoses, especially in girls and women, and while social media spreads both genuine recognition and misinformation, proper evaluation using DSM-5 criteria filters fad from fact
options.B: The colleague is entirely correct; social media is the sole cause of the rise
options.C: There is no way to know why diagnosis rates have changed
options.D: Overdiagnosis is impossible because ADHD evaluations never make mistakes

questions.explanation: The chapter's analysis has three parts: a real historical backlog (especially among girls and women) explains much of the surge, social media both triggers legitimate recognition and spreads misinformation, and rigorous DSM-5-based evaluation is the answer to sloppy diagnosis rather than dismissing the whole population. Option B credits a single cause the chapter treats as only partial. Option C ignores the chapter's detailed explanation. Option D overstates evaluation reliability, which the chapter never claims is perfect.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is true about who can diagnose ADHD, according to this chapter?

options.A: Psychiatrists, psychologists, and primary care providers can all diagnose ADHD, though each fits different situations best
options.B: Only psychiatrists are legally allowed to diagnose ADHD
options.C: Only a brain scan performed by a neurologist can confirm ADHD
options.D: Diagnosis requires a school principal's referral

questions.explanation: The chapter describes three main figures who can diagnose — psychiatrists, psychologists, and primary care providers — each best suited to different situations, from complex medication questions to straightforward childhood presentations. Option B wrongly excludes psychologists and PCPs. Option C is directly contradicted; no brain scan diagnoses ADHD. Option D invents a requirement the chapter never states.

questions.question_text: What does the "age of onset criterion" require for a valid ADHD diagnosis?

options.A: The person must be under 18 at the time of evaluation
options.B: Several symptoms must have been present before age 12
options.C: Symptoms must have appeared only in the last six months
options.D: The person must have failed a grade in school

questions.explanation: The age of onset criterion requires several symptoms to have been present before age 12, which is why old report cards and childhood memories matter so much in an evaluation. Option A confuses onset age with age at evaluation, which can be any age. Option C describes the opposite of a lifelong, early-starting pattern. Option D invents an unrelated academic requirement.

questions.question_text: What does a thorough evaluation report typically include, according to this chapter?

options.A: Only the final diagnostic code, with no further detail
options.B: A prescription only, without any written explanation
options.C: The referral question, procedures used, history summary, test scores if any, diagnostic conclusion, and recommendations
options.D: A guarantee of specific treatment outcomes

questions.explanation: The chapter describes a real evaluation report as containing the referral question, procedures used, a history summary, test scores if any, a diagnostic conclusion, and recommendations — a document meant to be read in full, not just for its last line. Option A describes a hollow report the chapter warns against. Option B confuses the report with a prescription. Option D overstates what any report can promise.

questions.question_text: Why does this chapter warn against relying on a continuous performance test (CPT) alone to diagnose ADHD?

options.A: CPTs are inaccurate for every person who takes them
options.B: CPTs are only available in research settings, not clinics
options.C: CPTs measure only long-term memory, which is irrelevant to ADHD
options.D: A quiet, novel computer task is a low-symptom setting, so many people with ADHD pass it while some without ADHD score poorly on a bad night — it's one data point, not the verdict

questions.explanation: The chapter explains that a quiet room with a novel computer task is precisely the low-symptom setting situational variability predicts, so CPT results alone are unreliable in either direction and should count as one data point among many. Option A overstates the test's unreliability across the board. Option B is factually wrong; CPTs are used clinically. Option C misdescribes what CPTs measure — sustained attention and impulsive responses, not long-term memory.

questions.question_text: Why does this chapter emphasize gathering collateral information, such as a partner's or teacher's input, during an evaluation?

options.A: People with ADHD are often imprecise self-observers, so information from people who see them daily corrects for under- or over-reporting
options.B: Collateral information replaces the need for a clinical interview entirely
options.C: Collateral information is only useful for children, never for adults
options.D: It is required only when the person being evaluated refuses to participate

questions.explanation: The chapter explains that self-monitoring is often weak in ADHD, so people under- or over-report their own symptoms, and collateral information from someone who observes them daily corrects for that gap. Option B wrongly treats collateral as a replacement rather than a complement to the interview. Option C is contradicted; the chapter explicitly extends collateral information to adult evaluations via partners. Option D invents a condition the chapter never states.

questions.question_text: How does this chapter resolve the tension between the underdiagnosis pattern and the overdiagnosis debate?

options.A: It concludes overdiagnosis is a myth invented by skeptics
options.B: It concludes underdiagnosis is a myth and only overdiagnosis is real
options.C: It holds that both failures are real and coexist, and the resolution to both is the same thing: thorough evaluations of the kind this chapter describes
options.D: It recommends abandoning diagnosis altogether given the uncertainty

questions.explanation: The chapter takes the position that sloppy quick diagnoses and massive missed populations both genuinely exist, and that thorough, well-structured evaluations resolve both problems at once. Option A and B each dismiss one real failure mode the chapter affirms. Option D contradicts the chapter's entire practical purpose of teaching readers to seek good evaluations.

questions.question_text: An online clinic offers "ADHD diagnosis in 30 minutes" based on a single attention test, with medication shipped the same week. Using this chapter's evaluation anatomy, what is the strongest concern?

options.A: Telehealth itself makes any evaluation invalid
options.B: It skips nearly every core component — real history-taking, childhood evidence, collateral information, and differential diagnosis — leaving only the least reliable single instrument
options.C: Same-week medication is illegal in all circumstances
options.D: Attention tests are never used in legitimate evaluations

questions.explanation: The chapter's checkbox exercise on this exact scenario finds nearly every component missing: no real interview, no childhood evidence, no collateral, no differential diagnosis, leaving only an attention-test-style instrument the chapter explicitly warns is unreliable alone. Option A is wrong; the chapter states telehealth done right is legitimate. Option C is not a claim the chapter makes about legality. Option D is false; attention tests are a common, legitimate component when used alongside everything else.

questions.question_text: A father hopes his son's new ADHD diagnosis will mean the school "excuses" missed homework and lowers expectations entirely. Based on what this chapter says a diagnosis does and does not mean, how should this expectation be corrected?

options.A: The diagnosis does mean exactly that — expectations should be dropped entirely
options.B: A diagnosis obligates the school to skip all consequences for any behavior
options.C: A diagnosis means the child no longer needs to attend school
options.D: A diagnosis names a real mechanism and opens doors to support, but it doesn't excuse behavior or predict outcomes; it changes the question to what the brain needs, not whether standards apply

questions.explanation: The chapter is explicit that a diagnosis does not mean the person is excused — it names a real mechanism and opens doors like accommodations and treatment, shifting the question from "why won't they?" to "what does this brain need?" rather than removing standards. Options A, B, and C all overstate the diagnosis as blanket exemption, which the chapter directly rejects.

questions.question_text: During an evaluation, a clinician asks only about the adult's current symptoms and skips any questions about childhood, report cards, or family history. Which component of a thorough evaluation is missing, and why does it matter?

options.A: Collateral information, because a partner should always attend every session
options.B: Neuropsychological testing, because it is required for every diagnosis
options.C: The childhood history requirement, because DSM-5 requires evidence that several symptoms were present before age 12 to distinguish ADHD from a recent-onset problem
options.D: The continuous performance test, because it is the most important instrument

questions.explanation: Skipping childhood history omits the evidence needed for the age-of-onset criterion, which distinguishes lifelong ADHD from a recently-developed problem with a different explanation. Option A misidentifies the missing piece as collateral information, which concerns present-day observers, not childhood evidence. Option B is wrong; the chapter states neuropsych testing is optional, not required. Option D wrongly elevates a single instrument the chapter treats as one data point among several.

questions.question_text: A woman is treated for years for anxiety, but her symptoms don't fully improve. A careful re-evaluation eventually finds underlying, unrecognized ADHD driving much of the anxiety. Using this chapter's concept of differential diagnosis, what does this case best illustrate?

options.A: Anxiety and ADHD can never occur in the same person
options.B: Differential diagnosis is rarely either/or — conditions can co-occur or one can be downstream of another, so ruling alternatives in or out, and in what order, is central diagnostic work
options.C: The original evaluation must have used a CPT, since that's the only way misdiagnosis happens
options.D: Once a person is diagnosed with anxiety, ADHD can be safely ruled out permanently

questions.explanation: The chapter describes differential diagnosis as rarely either/or — anxiety and ADHD can co-occur or one can be downstream of the other — so working out which condition is driving which struggle, and in what order to treat them, is the central diagnostic task, exactly as this case shows. Option A contradicts the chapter's explicit statement that ADHD and anxiety often co-occur. Option C invents a cause not stated in the case. Option D contradicts the entire point of ongoing differential diagnosis.

questions.question_text: What is comorbidity?

options.A: A rare complication only seen in severe ADHD
options.B: A term for ADHD that resolves on its own
options.C: The medical name for masking
options.D: Two or more conditions present in the same person at the same time

questions.explanation: Comorbidity is the medical term for two or more conditions present in the same person at the same time, and the chapter notes it's the norm in ADHD, not the exception, with roughly two-thirds of children affected. Option A wrongly limits it to severe cases. Option B misdescribes the term as a resolution rather than a co-presence. Option C confuses it with masking, an unrelated concept.

questions.question_text: What is ADHD burnout?

options.A: A rare complication only seen in severe ADHD
options.B: A period of profound exhaustion and functional collapse following months or years of masking and over-performance
options.C: A synonym for the DSM-5 diagnosis of ADHD
options.D: A mild form of ADHD that doesn't require treatment

questions.explanation: ADHD burnout is described as the crash at the end of an unsustainable compensation run — exhaustion, plummeting function, and emotional depletion after masking and over-performance, illustrated by Sana's collapse in her first job. Option A misstates it as a rare complication rather than a common pattern. Option C confuses it with the formal diagnosis itself. Option D understates its seriousness; the chapter treats it as a significant collapse, not a mild variant.

questions.question_text: According to this chapter, what structurally distinguishes bipolar disorder from ADHD?

options.A: Bipolar disorder is episodic — distinct periods of elevated or depressed mood as a departure from baseline — while ADHD traits are chronic and always-on
options.B: Bipolar disorder never involves sleep changes
options.C: ADHD is episodic while bipolar disorder is chronic and always-on
options.D: ADHD only affects children, while bipolar disorder only affects adults

questions.explanation: The chapter's distinguishing structure is time: ADHD traits are present since childhood and vary by situation, while bipolar disorder shows distinct episodes, days-to-weeks long, that depart from the person's baseline mood and energy. Option B is false; bipolar episodes often involve reduced need for sleep. Option C reverses the correct pattern. Option D contradicts the chapter's point that ADHD is a lifespan condition, not childhood-only.

questions.question_text: Why can a reading disability like dyslexia hide behind an ADHD diagnosis for years, according to this chapter?

options.A: Dyslexia and ADHD never occur in the same person, so there is no real confusion
options.B: Dyslexia only appears after adolescence, so it cannot be confused with childhood ADHD
options.C: Reading disabilities always improve on their own without any intervention
options.D: ADHD's missing homework can mask a reading problem, and a reading problem can look like inattention, since nobody focuses well on text they can't decode — the tell is domain-specific struggle

questions.explanation: The chapter describes mutual camouflage: ADHD's missed homework hides a reading problem, and unreadable text looks like an attention problem, with the real tell being struggle that craters one subject while sparing others. Option A contradicts the chapter's stated high co-occurrence rate. Option B is false; dyslexia can be present from early schooling. Option C contradicts the chapter's recommendation of testing and intervention.

questions.question_text: How does this chapter distinguish ADHD's discouragement from depression, at home?

options.A: Depression only occurs in people without ADHD
options.B: ADHD's discouragement is usually situational and interest-responsive, lighting up when something novel arrives, while depression flattens even the interesting things
options.C: ADHD discouragement and depression are identical and cannot be told apart
options.D: Depression is always caused directly by ADHD medication

questions.explanation: The chapter's key distinction is that ADHD's discouragement responds to novelty and interest, while depression flattens even things the person would normally enjoy, especially alongside hopelessness or withdrawal lasting weeks. Option A is false; depression co-occurs with ADHD at elevated rates. Option C collapses a distinction the chapter deliberately draws. Option D misattributes depression's cause to medication rather than the chronic-struggle pathway the chapter describes.

questions.question_text: According to this chapter, what determines whether defiant behavior in a child with ADHD reflects true oppositional defiant disorder rather than the "transition tax" and demand overload?

options.A: Whether the child is diagnosed with ADHD at all
options.B: Whether the parents use any form of discipline
options.C: Whether the defiance persists across all settings and relationships even after demands are adjusted and the relationship is repaired
options.D: Whether the child is male or female

questions.explanation: The chapter explains that much apparent opposition improves once ADHD is treated and the demand structure is repaired; true ODD is the pattern that persists across settings and relationships even after that repair. Option A conflates two separate diagnoses. Option B introduces an unrelated variable the chapter doesn't use as a distinguishing test. Option D has no basis in the chapter's discussion.

questions.question_text: Dev's parents assume his stimulant medication has "stopped working" because tenth grade is collapsing, and want a higher dose. Based on this chapter, what should happen first?

options.A: Re-screen for what else might be true — such as a reading disability or emerging low mood — before assuming the medication itself is the problem
options.B: Immediately double the medication dose without further evaluation
options.C: Stop all treatment since medication clearly cannot work long-term
options.D: Assume the original diagnosis must have been wrong

questions.explanation: The chapter's worked example shows Dev's collapse was actually driven by an undiagnosed reading disability and emerging low mood, not medication failure — the lesson is to re-screen before re-dosing. Option B jumps to a fix without checking the actual cause. Option C overreacts by abandoning treatment that was working. Option D wrongly discards an accurate original diagnosis.

questions.question_text: A teenager snores heavily and struggles with daytime fog and inattention. Which response best matches this chapter's guidance?

options.A: Immediately increase his ADHD stimulant dose to counter the fog
options.B: Assume the snoring is unrelated and only address the school performance
options.C: Treat it as a sleep-study referral for possible sleep apnea, since apnea can mimic ADHD outright rather than just adjusting stimulant medication
options.D: Dismiss it as normal teenage tiredness that needs no attention

questions.explanation: The chapter is explicit that snoring plus daytime fog is a sleep-study referral, not a stimulant adjustment, because sleep apnea can mimic ADHD outright. Option A treats the wrong system. Option B ignores a clearly connected symptom the chapter flags. Option D dismisses a pattern the chapter treats as clinically significant.

questions.question_text: A parent notices their teenager with ADHD has started mentioning thoughts of self-harm. According to this chapter's "when to seek help" guidance, what should happen?

options.A: Wait a few weeks to see if the feelings pass on their own
options.B: Address it immediately as a professional emergency, outranking every other concern in this book, such as by contacting 988 in the US
options.C: Treat it as a routine topic for the next scheduled ADHD follow-up appointment
options.D: Assume it's just a phase related to typical teenage moodiness and takes no action

questions.explanation: The chapter is unambiguous that any mention of self-harm or suicide is an immediate professional matter, naming 988 in the US, and states this outranks every other priority in the book. Option A delays action the chapter says should be immediate. Option C wrongly treats an emergency as routine. Option D dismisses a serious warning sign.

questions.question_text: A clinician is treating a patient who has both ADHD and severe, active suicidal thoughts. Using this chapter's treatment order principles, how should the clinician prioritize care?

options.A: Treat the ADHD first in all cases, since it is the root cause of everything else
options.B: Treat every condition in exactly the order they were diagnosed, regardless of severity
options.C: Ignore the suicidal thoughts entirely and focus only on functional improvement
options.D: Safety comes first — active suicidality outranks ADHD treatment and every other condition until it is addressed

questions.explanation: The chapter's treatment-order principles state plainly that safety comes first — active suicidality, an eating disorder at medical severity, or serious substance dependence outranks everything, ADHD included. Option A ignores the safety-first principle in favor of a rigid rule. Option B contradicts the chapter's point that order is reasoned per person, not fixed by diagnosis sequence. Option C is a dangerous dismissal the chapter would never support.

questions.question_text: What are the two classes of stimulant medications for ADHD?

options.A: SSRIs and SNRIs
options.B: Beta blockers and antihistamines
options.C: Methylphenidate and amphetamine medications
options.D: Sedatives and antipsychotics

questions.explanation: The chapter names exactly two stimulant classes — methylphenidate (Ritalin, Concerta) and amphetamine medications (Adderall, Vyvanse) — as close cousins with slightly different mechanisms. Options A, B, and D name unrelated medication categories not used as first-line ADHD stimulant treatments.

questions.question_text: What is titration, as this chapter defines it?

options.A: The deliberate process of finding the right medication and dose by starting low and adjusting stepwise while measuring response
options.B: A one-time test that determines a person's exact lifelong dose
options.C: A surgical procedure used to treat severe ADHD
options.D: The process of switching entirely from medication to therapy

questions.explanation: Titration is the stepwise process of starting low and adjusting medication and dose while measuring response, since the effective dose can only be found empirically for each individual nervous system. Option B wrongly treats it as a single test rather than an ongoing process. Option C misdescribes it as surgery. Option D confuses it with an unrelated treatment switch.

questions.question_text: What does this chapter mean by "pills don't build skills"?

options.A: Medication has no effect on ADHD symptoms whatsoever
options.B: Only non-stimulant medications are effective; stimulants are placebo
options.C: Skills-based treatment always works better than medication
options.D: Medication can improve executive functioning for some hours a day, but it doesn't install routines, teach planning, or organize a backpack — systems and skills still need to be built separately

questions.explanation: The chapter is clear that medication can improve steerable attention for part of the day, but it doesn't teach planning or build routines — those come from the systems in later chapters, working alongside medication rather than being replaced by it. Option A contradicts the chapter's strong evidence base for medication's effect. Option B misrepresents stimulants as ineffective. Option C makes an unsupported ranking claim the chapter never makes.

questions.question_text: How do stimulant medications work in the brain, according to this chapter?

options.A: They sedate the brain broadly, reducing all activity equally
options.B: They mainly block dopamine (and norepinephrine) reuptake, or boost release, strengthening signaling in prefrontal and reward circuits that under-serve regulation
options.C: They permanently rewire neural pathways within a single dose
options.D: They work by suppressing appetite, which indirectly improves focus

questions.explanation: The chapter explains that methylphenidate blocks dopamine and norepinephrine reuptake while amphetamines also boost release, both strengthening signaling in the prefrontal and reward circuits Chapter 2 identified as under-serving regulation. Option A misdescribes stimulants as sedating rather than improving steering. Option C overstates a same-day chemical effect as permanent rewiring. Option D reverses cause and effect; appetite suppression is a side effect, not the mechanism of action.

questions.question_text: What does this chapter say in response to the misconception "stimulant medication is basically legal meth"?

options.A: The claim is entirely accurate and families should be alarmed
options.B: Stimulant medications contain no similar compounds to any illegal drug
options.C: The molecules are related, but medical formulations, doses, and delivery are engineered exactly opposite to abuse pharmacology, with slow delivery as a safety feature
options.D: This concern only applies to non-stimulant medications

questions.explanation: The chapter acknowledges the molecules are related but explains that medical dosing and slow-delivery formulations are engineered specifically to avoid abuse pharmacology, which is itself a safety feature. Option A overstates the concern as fully valid. Option B denies a chemical relationship the chapter acknowledges. Option D misapplies a stimulant-specific misconception to non-stimulants, which aren't controlled substances at all.

questions.question_text: Why does a disappointing first trial of one stimulant class mean less than families often fear, according to this chapter?

options.A: Because response is individual by class, and a person who responds poorly to one class quite often does well on the other — trying the other class is a standard next step
options.B: Because medication never actually works for ADHD
options.C: Because all stimulants are chemically identical regardless of class
options.D: Because a disappointing trial always means the diagnosis was wrong

questions.explanation: The chapter states that response is individual by class, so a poor result on one class often doesn't predict the other, making "try the other class" a standard, low-stakes next move. Option B contradicts the chapter's strong evidence base for stimulant effectiveness. Option C is factually wrong; the two classes work through related but distinct mechanisms. Option D wrongly ties medication response to diagnostic accuracy, which the chapter treats as separate questions.

questions.question_text: A father notices his daughter becomes irritable and flat every day right around 5 pm, and assumes she's "reverting to her old self." Based on this chapter, what is the more accurate explanation?

options.A: She is choosing to misbehave on purpose each evening
options.B: Her ADHD diagnosis must have been incorrect
options.C: The medication is permanently changing her personality
options.D: This is likely end-of-dose rebound or wear-off, a predictable pharmacokinetic event tied to when the medication exits her system, not a character reversion

questions.explanation: The chapter explicitly names the "5 pm cliff" as end-of-dose rebound — a real, schedulable pharmacokinetic event, not a character reversion. Option A misreads a physiological pattern as intentional behavior. Option B conflates a dosing effect with diagnostic accuracy. Option C overstates a temporary daily pattern as a permanent personality change.

questions.question_text: A family repeatedly struggles because their teen's stimulant prescription can't be refilled early and requires a new prescription every month with ID checks at the pharmacy. Which approach does this chapter recommend?

options.A: Ask the pharmacy to bend the rules as a one-time favor each month
options.B: Treat the refill logistics as a system to design around from day one — calendar alarms for reorder day, pharmacy apps, and an agreed family reminder protocol
options.C: Switch to an unregulated substitute purchased without a prescription
options.D: Give up on the medication because the rules are too burdensome to manage

questions.explanation: The chapter recommends treating Schedule II refill logistics as a system to build from day one, including calendar alarms and an agreed family reminder protocol, since the rules demand exactly the executive function ADHD makes hard. Option A is not a realistic or recommended workaround. Option C is unsafe and never suggested. Option D abandons a working treatment over a solvable logistics problem.

questions.question_text: Two weeks into a stimulant trial, a child is finishing homework without conflict, but is flat at dinner, eating little, and staying up past 11 pm. Her parent wants to stop the medication entirely. Based on this chapter, what is the recommended next step?

options.A: Stop the medication immediately and never revisit medication as an option
options.B: Ignore the flatness and appetite changes since the homework result alone proves success
options.C: Record all the changes with times of day, report them fully to the prescriber, and let the titration process adjust the dose or timing rather than ending the trial early
options.D: Double the dose immediately to see if the homework improvement gets even stronger

questions.explanation: The chapter treats every symptom in this scenario as a titration signal — recorded with times of day and reported to the prescriber, so the process can adjust dose or timing rather than the trial being abandoned or escalated unilaterally. Option A discards real target-symptom progress unnecessarily. Option B ignores side effects the chapter treats as significant. Option D is a unilateral dose change that should go through the prescriber, not the family.

questions.question_text: A family weighing whether to try medication worries that starting it means committing to a permanent, irreversible path. Using this chapter's framing, how should they best analyze this concern?

options.A: A stimulant trial is closer to a reversible experiment than a permanent life choice, since same-day pharmacology means stopping returns the person to baseline, and the real comparison is medication versus the costs of the status quo, not medication versus nothing
options.B: The concern is accurate; once started, stimulant medication cannot be stopped
options.C: Medication decisions, once made, should never be revisited at any later life stage
options.D: The only responsible choice is to avoid medication entirely to prevent any risk

questions.explanation: The chapter reframes the decision three ways: a stimulant trial is reversible because effects don't accumulate day to day, the real comparison is against the status quo's own costs (burnout, chronic stress), and the decision is renewable at every life stage. Option B and C both wrongly treat the decision as permanent and unrevisitable, which the chapter directly rejects. Option D swaps one blanket answer for another instead of weighing the actual trade-offs.

questions.question_text: What does "multimodal treatment" mean in this chapter?

options.A: Combining several kinds of intervention — such as medication, skills-based therapy, family training, and lifestyle foundations — rather than relying on one alone
options.B: Using only medication, since guidelines say it's the single most effective option
options.C: Switching between different medications until one works
options.D: Treating only the co-occurring conditions and ignoring ADHD itself

questions.explanation: Multimodal treatment means combining medication (if chosen), skills-based therapy, family training, school or workplace supports, and lifestyle foundations, since no single intervention touches every system ADHD affects. Option B contradicts the chapter's "portfolio, not silver bullet" framing. Option C confuses multimodal treatment with medication titration. Option D wrongly excludes ADHD itself from the treatment plan.

questions.question_text: Why does this chapter treat psychoeducation as a genuine first-line treatment rather than just background reading?

options.A: It has no real evidence behind it but is included for completeness
options.B: Psychoeducation is only useful after all other treatments have failed
options.C: Structured, accurate understanding of ADHD changes behavior directly — parents stop issuing surprise demands, couples stop moralizing forgetfulness — and guidelines list it as a first step of care
options.D: It replaces the need for any professional evaluation

questions.explanation: The chapter argues that accurate models of ADHD directly change behavior — citing the transition tax, delay aversion, and prospective memory examples — and notes guidelines list psychoeducation as a genuine first step, not merely background reading. Option A understates its evidence base. Option B misplaces it as a last resort rather than a first step. Option D overstates its role; it complements, not replaces, evaluation.

questions.question_text: From lowest to highest, how does this chapter's treatment evidence hierarchy rank types of evidence?

options.A: Meta-analyses, randomized controlled trials, observational studies, expert opinion, anecdotes and testimonials
options.B: Anecdotes and testimonials, expert opinion, observational studies, randomized controlled trials, meta-analyses
options.C: Randomized controlled trials, anecdotes, meta-analyses, expert opinion, observational studies
options.D: All forms of evidence are treated as equally reliable in this hierarchy

questions.explanation: The chapter ranks anecdotes and testimonials lowest, then expert opinion, then observational studies, then randomized controlled trials, with meta-analyses at the summit. Option A reverses the order. Option C scrambles the ranking so randomized trials and anecdotes are placed inconsistently. Option D directly contradicts the entire point of having a hierarchy.

questions.question_text: Why do major guidelines recommend behavioral parent training before medication for preschool-age children with ADHD?

options.A: Because medication is unsafe at any age
options.B: Because parent training and medication can never be combined later
options.C: Because preschoolers do not actually have ADHD
options.D: Because parent training has excellent evidence and equips parents with technical skills for redesigning daily structure, making it a strong first step for young children specifically

questions.explanation: The chapter states parent training's evidence is excellent and describes it as technical training in redesigning daily structure — clear expectations, effective instructions, consistent reinforcement — making it the recommended first step for preschoolers specifically. Option A overstates medication's risk profile beyond what the chapter claims. Option B contradicts the chapter's portfolio approach, which combines interventions over time. Option C contradicts the chapter's premise that preschoolers can have ADHD.

questions.question_text: What is the honest verdict on neurofeedback, according to this chapter?

options.A: It has been thoroughly proven effective in every well-controlled trial
options.B: It is dangerous and should never be attempted under any circumstances
options.C: Results are mixed, and the better-controlled the trial, the smaller the effect gets — a pattern consistent with placebo-plus-practice rather than specific efficacy
options.D: It works identically to medication and can fully replace it

questions.explanation: The chapter's unsparing summary is that neurofeedback's apparent effects shrink as trial controls improve, especially with sham-feedback comparisons — the classic signature of placebo-plus-practice. Option A reverses the actual pattern of the evidence. Option B overstates safety concerns; the chapter calls it generally safe, just not well-supported as core treatment. Option D contradicts the chapter's explicit warning against using it instead of evidence-based care.

questions.question_text: What is the honest verdict on omega-3 supplementation for ADHD, according to this chapter?

options.A: Meta-analyses find a real but small benefit — worth discussing as a low-risk add-on, but not a substitute for medication
options.B: It has zero effect and should never be considered
options.C: It is more effective than any stimulant medication
options.D: It is banned by major medical guidelines

questions.explanation: The chapter gives omega-3 an honest middle verdict: meta-analyses show a real but small benefit, reasonable as a low-risk add-on discussed with a clinician, but nowhere near a medication substitute. Option B understates its documented small effect. Option C dramatically overstates its efficacy compared to stimulants. Option D is not a claim the chapter makes.

questions.question_text: A college student with ADHD says her main struggle is keeping up with a weekly schedule and remembering deadlines, not underlying anxious thoughts or family conflict. Which approach from this chapter's table best fits her stated need?

options.A: Behavioral parent training
options.B: Neurofeedback
options.C: A supplement stack marketed as a natural focus booster
options.D: ADHD coaching, which works on this week's actual logistics, schedules, and accountability

questions.explanation: The chapter's table matches ADHD coaching to students and adults needing scaffolding and logistics support rather than therapy, which is exactly her stated need. Behavioral parent training (A) targets parents raising children, not the student herself. Neurofeedback (B) has weak controlled evidence and isn't matched to logistics support. A supplement stack (C) is a marketplace claim the chapter warns against, not a matched treatment approach.

questions.question_text: A family is considering a marketed "ADHD supplement blend" advertised as "doctor formulated" with many testimonials but no cited studies. Using this chapter's evaluating treatment claims framework, what should they do?

options.A: Buy it immediately, since testimonials from real customers are strong evidence
options.B: Ask what evidence supports it beyond testimonials, note that US supplements aren't required to prove efficacy before sale, and weigh the cost against stronger-evidence options
options.C: Assume the FDA has already verified its effectiveness before allowing it to be sold
options.D: Refuse to consider any supplement under any circumstances, regardless of the specific evidence

questions.explanation: The chapter's framework asks what evidence exists beyond testimonials, reminds readers that US supplements don't need proven efficacy before sale, and weighs cost against the "compared to what" question of stronger-evidence alternatives. Option A treats the weakest evidence tier as strong. Option C misunderstands US supplement regulation, which the chapter explicitly corrects. Option D overcorrects into a blanket rule the chapter doesn't recommend, since it allows omega-3 as a reasonable low-risk add-on.

questions.question_text: A family starts their child in neurofeedback sessions without deciding in advance what improvement would justify continuing. Based on this chapter's guidance on measuring treatment progress, what should they have done differently?

options.A: Define target outcomes and a review date with a real decision in mind — continue, adjust, or stop — before starting, especially for contested treatments like neurofeedback
options.B: Nothing; neurofeedback doesn't require any tracking since its evidence is already conclusive
options.C: Wait until year two to consider whether it's working
options.D: Only judge progress based on how the child feels about the sessions emotionally

questions.explanation: The chapter specifically recommends pre-committing to target outcomes and a review date before starting contested treatments, deciding in advance what would justify continuing rather than letting sunk cost and hope drive the decision. Option B wrongly assumes neurofeedback's evidence removes the need for tracking. Option C delays evaluation far longer than the chapter's monthly-timescale recommendation. Option D ignores the structured, observable outcomes the chapter calls for.

questions.question_text: A clinic advertises a bundled "12-week ADHD reset" combining neurofeedback, a custom supplement stack, and weekly coaching for a high fixed price, citing "hundreds of success stories" as its evidence. Applying this chapter's evidence hierarchy and consumer-training framework, what is the strongest analysis?

options.A: Because the bundle includes coaching, which has real value, the entire package is well-supported
options.B: Success stories from hundreds of people are equivalent to a randomized controlled trial
options.C: The claim rests on testimonial-level evidence, bundles a contested therapy and an unproven supplement with a genuinely useful but unregulated service, and the same money would buy more higher-evidence care if spent separately — the "compared to what" question exposes the real cost
options.D: Because the price is high, the treatment must be more effective than lower-cost options

questions.explanation: The chapter's own worked example of a nearly identical bundle applies exactly this analysis: testimonial-floor evidence, bundling that obscures which component is doing anything, and a "compared to what" question showing the same money buys more higher-evidence care elsewhere. Option A wrongly lets one legitimate component vouch for the whole bundle. Option B conflates the lowest and highest tiers of the evidence hierarchy. Option D assumes price tracks effectiveness, which the chapter never claims.

questions.question_text: What does "externalizing memory" mean in this chapter?

options.A: Memorizing information more thoroughly through repetition
options.B: Relying entirely on someone else to remember things for you
options.C: Moving information out of your head and into reliable external storage — paper, phone, alarms — the moment it arrives
options.D: A medical procedure that improves memory function

questions.explanation: Externalizing memory means moving information out of your head into reliable external storage the instant it arrives, patching working memory's leaks and prospective memory's unreliable alarm. Option A describes the opposite approach, relying more on internal memory. Option B misplaces the responsibility onto another person rather than an external system. Option D confuses a practical technique with a medical intervention.

questions.question_text: What is body doubling?

options.A: Doing your work in the presence of another person who is simply there, without them helping or supervising
options.B: Assigning two people to complete the same task independently for comparison
options.C: A therapy technique where a therapist mimics the client's behavior
options.D: Scheduling two accountability partners instead of one

questions.explanation: Body doubling means working in the presence of another person who is simply there doing their own thing, supplying mild arousal and social presence without supervision or help. Option B describes parallel task assignment, not shared presence. Option C invents an unrelated clinical technique. Option D confuses body doubling with the separate concept of accountability partners.

questions.question_text: What is the Pomodoro technique, as described in this chapter?

options.A: A method of preparing meals in advance to save time
options.B: A type of alarm that only rings once per day
options.C: A technique for permanently eliminating the need for breaks
options.D: Committing to one task for a fixed sprint (classically 25 minutes), followed by a short timed break, repeated

questions.explanation: The Pomodoro technique packages timers into a work rhythm: a fixed sprint, classically 25 minutes, followed by a short timed break, repeated with longer breaks every few cycles. Option A is an unrelated meal-planning concept. Option B misdescribes it as a single alarm rather than a repeating rhythm. Option C is the opposite of the technique, which deliberately builds in sanctioned breaks.

questions.question_text: Why does the chapter say alarms and timers should be labeled with their action (such as "PHARMACY before home") rather than left blank?

options.A: Labels are not actually necessary; any alarm works the same way
options.B: Labels are required by phone manufacturers
options.C: An unlabeled alarm firing later becomes a mystery rather than an instruction, since the intention behind it was never externalized in a retrievable form
options.D: Labeled alarms play a different sound than unlabeled ones

questions.explanation: The chapter stresses that an unlabeled alarm going off later is a mystery, not an instruction — labeling the alarm with its action is what makes externalization actually work at the moment it's needed. Option A contradicts the chapter's explicit advice. Option B invents an unrelated technical requirement. Option D is a fabricated claim about alarm sounds.
