questions.question_text: Why does this chapter recommend anchoring routines to an existing fixed event (like "after the coffee finishes") rather than a specific clock time (like "at 7:15")?

options.A: An event-anchored cue survives schedule disruptions like weekends, while a clock-time cue is more fragile and easily missed
options.B: Clock times are technically impossible to use for routines
options.C: Anchoring to events is required by law in some states
options.D: Clock times work better for people with ADHD than event anchors do

questions.explanation: The chapter explains that "after the coffee finishes" survives weekends and schedule changes, while "at 7:15" is a more fragile cue that's easy to miss when the day's rhythm shifts. Option B is factually false; clock times can be used, just less reliably for this purpose. Option C is an invented and irrelevant claim. Option D reverses the chapter's actual recommendation.

questions.question_text: Why does defining a concrete "next action" (like "find the renewal notice and put it by the laptop") often break through weeks of stalled procrastination, according to this chapter?

options.A: Because it makes the task more important than it was before
options.B: Because most stalled procrastination is actually an undefined next action — the starter motor has nothing sized correctly to grab, and a small, concrete, decision-free step gives it something to start
options.C: Because writing anything down guarantees task completion
options.D: Because next actions eliminate the need to ever finish the larger project

questions.explanation: The chapter argues that most procrastination on projects is an undefined next action problem — the starter motor needs something specific and small enough to grab, illustrated by the ninety-second registration renewal example. Option A misattributes the mechanism to perceived importance. Option C overstates what mere writing accomplishes without concreteness. Option D confuses a starting step with skipping the rest of the project.

questions.question_text: A parent wants to help their teenager start using a planner. Based on this chapter's guidance, which approach fits best?

options.A: Buy an elaborate planner as a surprise gift and expect the teen to adopt it immediately
options.B: Set up every feature of the planner in one sitting to save time later
options.C: Require the teen to use the planner exactly as designed with no adjustments allowed
options.D: Build the system together with the teen's input, starting with one small piece like a daily three-item list, rather than imposing a complete system all at once

questions.explanation: The chapter's closing diagnosis of a failed planner gift stresses that systems built with the person, starting small and added to gradually, succeed where imposed, all-at-once systems collapse. Option A describes exactly the imposed-gift pattern the chapter diagnoses as a common failure. Option B risks the "installed everything at once" collapse the chapter warns about. Option C removes the tinkering and iteration the chapter treats as essential.

questions.question_text: A person wants to stop reaching for their phone during homework time. Which environment design move from this chapter best fits this goal?

options.A: Leave the phone on the desk but ask themselves to resist checking it through willpower alone
options.B: Charge the phone in the kitchen during homework time, so distraction requires extra physical effort to reach
options.C: Delete all apps from the phone permanently
options.D: Set a phone alarm reminding them not to check the phone

questions.explanation: The chapter's environment design principle is to add friction to the wrong things — charging the phone in the kitchen during homework is exactly the kind of friction-adding move it recommends. Option A relies on willpower, which the chapter explicitly argues systems should replace. Option C is a far more drastic step than the chapter suggests. Option D uses the phone itself as the reminder, undermining the whole point of removing it from reach.

questions.question_text: Someone has a today-list with forty items and feels paralyzed every morning looking at it. Based on this chapter, what is the recommended fix?

options.A: Add even more items to make sure nothing is forgotten
options.B: Memorize the forty items instead of writing them down
options.C: Keep a separate everything-list, but limit today's actual list to three-to-five items, physically separated from the larger list
options.D: Complete all forty items in a single day through sheer effort

questions.explanation: The chapter's rule for to-do lists that work is keeping today's list to three-to-five items, physically separate from the everything-list, since a forty-item list produces decision paralysis and daily non-completion shame. Option A worsens the exact problem described. Option B contradicts the externalization principle underlying the whole chapter. Option D is an unrealistic demand the chapter never recommends.

questions.question_text: A person, newly excited about this chapter, installs a capture app, a new to-do list system, an estimation log, a Pomodoro timer, a body-doubling schedule, and a full morning and evening routine all in the same weekend. By Thursday, none of it is being used. Using this chapter's analysis, what best explains the collapse?

options.A: Installing many new systems at once collides with the novelty curve and habit fragility this chapter describes; the fix is one system at a time, rebuilt smaller after any collapse, not abandoned as a character failure
options.B: The person simply lacks the willpower required to maintain systems
options.C: None of these systems actually work for anyone with ADHD
options.D: The collapse proves the person doesn't actually want to improve

questions.explanation: The chapter names this exact pattern as the classic failure mode: installing every system in one inspired weekend collides with the novelty curve and the fragility of new habits, and the fix is starting with one system at a time and rebuilding smaller after a collapse. Option B revives the willpower myth the book has already retired. Option C overgeneralizes from a design mistake to blanket ineffectiveness. Option D wrongly reads a predictable systems failure as a statement about motivation or desire.

questions.question_text: Why does this chapter consider digital calendars the highest-value digital tool for ADHD?

options.A: They require no setup at all
options.B: They are the only tool proven to work for every person with ADHD
options.C: They fire and interrupt on schedule, unlike a paper calendar that must be remembered to be checked
options.D: They automatically complete tasks on your behalf

questions.explanation: The chapter's mechanical reason is that digital calendars fire and interrupt on schedule, while a paper calendar depends on being remembered to be checked — exactly the prospective memory failure point this book keeps returning to. Option A overstates ease of use as the reason. Option B claims a universality the chapter never asserts. Option D wildly overstates what a calendar does.

questions.question_text: What is deadline scaffolding?

options.A: Splitting a project into staged mini-deadlines, each attached to a witness or consequence, since distant deadlines are motivationally invisible
options.B: Waiting until the final deadline and working through the night
options.C: A type of physical furniture used to organize paperwork
options.D: Asking a supervisor to permanently remove all deadlines

questions.explanation: Deadline scaffolding manufactures near deadlines out of a distant one by splitting a project into staged mini-deadlines, each needing a witness or consequence to actually function. Option B describes the exact pattern scaffolding is designed to prevent. Option C is a literal misreading of "scaffolding." Option D contradicts the chapter's point that deadlines are manufactured, not eliminated.

questions.question_text: According to this chapter's discussion of system maintenance, what happens to every organizational system over time?

options.A: A well-designed system, once built correctly, never needs any further attention
options.B: Systems only fail for people who don't truly want to be organized
options.C: Only digital systems decay; paper-based systems last indefinitely
options.D: Every system will eventually stop working as novelty fuel burns down, and this is normal operation, not failure

questions.explanation: The chapter's central claim about maintenance is that every system eventually stops working as novelty burns down, and that this is normal operation requiring a maintenance loop, not evidence of failure. Option A contradicts the chapter's entire argument for ongoing maintenance. Option B revives a character-based explanation the chapter rejects. Option C is false; the chapter notes even shared calendars and paper planners decay without upkeep.

questions.question_text: Why does this chapter recommend "selective visibility" rather than standard minimalism advice when decluttering for ADHD?

options.A: Because clutter has no real effect on attention or cognitive load
options.B: Because minimalism is only appropriate for people without ADHD
options.C: Because aggressive tidying can effectively delete working systems — items "put away nicely" become functionally invisible and forgotten — so active surfaces should be cleared while action items stay visible on purpose
options.D: Because every object in a room should always remain visible at all times

questions.explanation: The chapter explains that out-of-sight is genuinely out-of-mind for this brain, so tidying away action items can delete a working system — the fix is clearing active surfaces while deliberately keeping action items visible. Option A contradicts the chapter's explicit mechanism linking clutter to attention and load. Option B is an unsupported blanket claim. Option D overcorrects into permanent visibility for everything, which the chapter doesn't recommend for storage items.

questions.question_text: Why does this chapter recommend layering multiple distraction defenses (distance, friction, silence, urgency) rather than relying on one?

options.A: Because each single defense tends to fail independently at different moments, while a stack of layers degrades gracefully, since one layer usually catches what another misses
options.B: Because a single defense is illegal to use alone
options.C: Because using more than one defense doubles a person's willpower
options.D: Because layering defenses eliminates all distraction completely with no failures

questions.explanation: The chapter's Omar example shows that any single layer fails weekly, but the stack fails rarely, because when one layer fails another usually still catches the drift. Option B is a fabricated claim. Option C misattributes the mechanism to willpower, which the chapter treats as an unreliable strategy. Option D overstates the result; the chapter is explicit that defenses reduce, never eliminate, distraction.

questions.question_text: What does "momentum and activation" mean in this chapter, and how does the five-minute contract use it?

options.A: Starting and continuing a task cost the same amount of effort, so the five-minute contract makes no real difference
options.B: For ADHD, starting is the expensive part while continuing is nearly free once moving, so committing to just five minutes with permission to quit lowers the barrier enough to begin
options.C: Momentum only applies to physical exercise, not cognitive tasks
options.D: The five-minute contract is a trick that never actually leads to longer work sessions

questions.explanation: The chapter explains that starting is the expensive part of any task for ADHD, while continuing is nearly free once moving — the five-minute contract exploits this by making the barrier small enough to cross, with permission to quit honored on the times it's invoked. Option A denies the asymmetry the chapter's whole argument rests on. Option C narrows the concept to an unrelated domain. Option D contradicts the chapter's observation that most sessions continue past five minutes.

questions.question_text: Someone has an overwhelming everything-list and doesn't know what to prioritize this morning. Using this chapter's one-question shortcut, what should they ask?

options.A: What would look most impressive to complete first?
options.B: What is the most enjoyable item on the list?
options.C: What has been on the list the longest?
options.D: What, left undone, causes the most damage by Friday?

questions.explanation: The chapter's shortcut for overwhelmed mornings is exactly this question — what, left undone, causes the most damage by Friday — with everything else treated as genuinely negotiable. Option A substitutes appearance for actual consequence. Option B lets interest override importance, which the chapter warns distorts ADHD prioritization. Option C uses list tenure as a stand-in for actual stakes, which the chapter doesn't recommend.

questions.question_text: A parent wants to set up a reward for their child after completing a long, boring homework session, following this chapter's reward system design principles. Which approach fits best?

options.A: Promise a large reward at the end of the school year for consistent effort
options.B: Offer a small, immediate reward right after the session, written on the list in advance, and actually deliver it every time
options.C: Only mention the reward if the child specifically asks for one
options.D: Give the reward randomly, sometimes before the work and sometimes long after, to keep it interesting

questions.explanation: The chapter's redesign calls for rewards that are immediate and small, visible in advance, and actually collected every time — distant rewards don't motivate an ADHD reward system. Option A relies on exactly the distant-reward structure the chapter says fails. Option C removes the advance visibility the chapter treats as essential. Option D introduces unreliable timing that would teach the system the reward is fake.

questions.question_text: A person set up a complete distraction-blocking system in September, and by November it has completely fallen apart — blockers uninstalled, notifications back on, ritual abandoned. Based on this chapter's guidance, what should they do?

options.A: Conclude the whole approach is worthless and never try any system again
options.B: Rebuild the exact same elaborate system from scratch with no changes
options.C: Hold a "cheerful funeral" for the collapsed system, harvest the parts that worked, and rebuild a smaller version while adding a missing weekly maintenance review
options.D: Blame themselves for lacking the discipline to maintain any system

questions.explanation: The chapter's exact answer to this scenario is to hold a cheerful funeral, keep what worked, rebuild shrunk, and add the missing weekly maintenance review so the next decay gets caught early. Option A overgeneralizes one collapse into total failure. Option B ignores the lesson that rebuilding smaller, not identically, is the effective move. Option D revives the character-blame framing the chapter explicitly rejects.

questions.question_text: A family notices that whenever one of their household systems (a chore chart, a calendar, a blocker) stops working, they immediately conclude "we're just not organized people" and give up on systems entirely for months. Using this chapter's analysis of system maintenance, what is the deeper flaw in their response?

options.A: They are treating normal, expected system decay as a permanent character verdict, when the chapter's framing is that systems are perishable and maintenance — not personal failure — is what keeps a household running long-term
options.B: They are correct; repeated system failure proves the family isn't capable of being organized
options.C: The only solution is to hire a professional organizer instead of building any systems themselves
options.D: Digital systems would solve this problem permanently, since they never decay

questions.explanation: The chapter's whole argument is that systems are perishable by design, and the households that stay functional are the ones that treat maintenance as normal Tuesday work rather than reading each collapse as a character verdict. Option B accepts the flawed conclusion the chapter is directly arguing against. Option C skips past the maintenance skill the chapter says any family can learn. Option D contradicts the chapter's explicit statement that even digital tools like calendars can decay without upkeep, just less easily.

questions.question_text: What is emotional dysregulation, as this chapter defines it?

options.A: A rare complication that only affects a small minority of people with ADHD
options.B: The complete absence of emotional response
options.C: A formal DSM-5 diagnostic category separate from ADHD
options.D: Emotions that arrive faster, hit harder, and take longer to release than the situation calls for

questions.explanation: Emotional dysregulation is emotions that arrive faster, hit harder, and take longer to release than the situation calls for — the chapter treats it as part of ADHD's core machinery, not a side effect. Option A understates how common and central it is. Option B describes the opposite of dysregulation. Option C misplaces it as a separate DSM category rather than a feature of ADHD itself.

questions.question_text: What is rejection sensitive dysphoria (RSD)?

options.A: A community-coined term for disproportionate, sometimes physically painful emotional collapse in response to rejection, criticism, or perceived failure
options.B: A formal DSM-5 diagnosis that always accompanies ADHD
options.C: A medication side effect specific to non-stimulants
options.D: The clinical term for hyperactivity in adults

questions.explanation: RSD is a community-coined term, not a formal diagnosis, describing a disproportionate emotional collapse in response to rejection, criticism, or even perceived or imagined failure, arriving as fact rather than as a thought. Option B wrongly treats it as an official diagnosis. Option C misplaces it as a medication effect. Option D confuses it with an unrelated symptom category.

questions.question_text: How does this chapter distinguish guilt from shame?

options.A: Guilt and shame are simply two words for the same experience
options.B: Guilt only occurs in children, while shame only occurs in adults
options.C: Guilt says "I did a bad thing" and tends to repair, while shame says "I am the bad thing" and tends to corrode, hide, and avoid
options.D: Shame is always a healthy motivator, while guilt is always harmful

questions.explanation: The chapter draws a sharp line: guilt is about an action and drives repair, while shame is about identity and drives hiding, avoidance, and corrosion — illustrated by the unopened mail and the unstarted project. Option A collapses a distinction the chapter treats as essential. Option B invents an age restriction not in the text. Option D reverses the chapter's actual evaluation of the two emotions.

questions.question_text: Why does "pausing before reacting" work as a regulation skill, according to this chapter?

options.A: Because thinking about a problem for an hour always resolves it completely
options.B: Because pausing eliminates the possibility of ever feeling upset again
options.C: Because a pause guarantees the triggering concern was imaginary
options.D: Because an emotional surge typically peaks and begins to fall within roughly ninety seconds if it isn't re-fueled by further action, so buying that time lets it decay

questions.explanation: The chapter explains the surge peaks and begins falling within about ninety seconds if not re-fueled by action like sending an angry text, so mechanical tools like the drafts-folder rule exist purely to buy that window. Option A overstates what a pause accomplishes. Option B claims an impossible permanent effect. Option C wrongly assumes the underlying concern is always false, which the chapter explicitly says isn't the point.

questions.question_text: According to this chapter, why does self-compassion improve follow-through rather than lowering standards?

options.A: Because shame drives hiding and avoidance, while decency and self-compassion leave enough safety for a person to try again
options.B: Because self-compassion has no measurable effect on behavior at all
options.C: Because self-compassion means never holding oneself accountable for anything
options.D: Because self-compassion only works for people without ADHD

questions.explanation: The chapter cites research showing self-compassion improves follow-through because shame drives hiding and avoidance, while decency toward oneself leaves enough psychological safety to try again. Option B contradicts the evidence the chapter cites. Option C confuses self-compassion with the absence of accountability, which the chapter never claims. Option D invents an unsupported restriction.

questions.question_text: What does this chapter identify as the two common failure modes in "identity after diagnosis," and what is the more stable landing between them?

options.A: The failure modes are laziness and overachievement; the stable landing is perfect balance between the two
options.B: The failure modes are over-merger (ADHD becomes the whole identity) and rejection (refusing the label entirely); the stable landing treats ADHD as load-bearing context, not the whole self
options.C: The only failure mode is refusing treatment; the stable landing is always taking medication
options.D: The failure modes only apply to children, never to adults

questions.explanation: The chapter names over-merger and rejection as the two sandbars, with the stable landing being ADHD as load-bearing context — one important fact among many, rather than the whole identity. Option A invents unrelated failure modes. Option C narrows identity work to a treatment choice, which is a separate topic. Option D is false; the chapter discusses this process primarily in the context of late-diagnosed adults.

questions.question_text: A friend texts back a brief "ok" and the recipient immediately feels certain the friendship is over. Using this chapter's cognitive reframing skill, what is the recommended response?

options.A: Immediately confront the friend about ending the friendship
options.B: Assume the catastrophic reading is definitely correct, since RSD alarms are always accurate
options.C: Generate at least one alternative reading (such as "she's driving") and hold both possibilities until real evidence arrives, rather than acting on the catastrophic interpretation alone
options.D: Avoid all future contact with the friend to prevent further hurt

questions.explanation: Cognitive reframing means generating one alternative reading and holding both interpretations as hypotheses until evidence arrives, exactly the "ok" text example the chapter uses. Option A acts on the catastrophic reading without checking it. Option B contradicts the chapter's point that RSD alarms are false at least half the time. Option D overcorrects into avoidance, which the chapter never recommends.

questions.question_text: Someone wants to ask their manager for deadlines instead of vague timelines, using this chapter's "mechanism → pattern → ask" formula for explaining their ADHD. Which statement best follows that formula?

options.A: "I have ADHD, which is a neurodevelopmental disorder defined by inattention and hyperactivity-impulsivity that begins in childhood."
options.B: "My brain doesn't cue me at the right moment, which is why I miss things I care about — deadlines land better than 'whenever' for me. Could you give me a real date?"
options.C: "Sorry to bother you, but I sometimes struggle with things, so please be patient with me in general."
options.D: "I can't help forgetting things, so it's not really my responsibility if deadlines get missed."

questions.explanation: This is the chapter's own worked formula — one sentence of mechanism, one of pattern, one specific ask — delivered without apology or medical lecture. Option A is a clinical definition, not a mechanism-pattern-ask statement suited to a workplace conversation. Option C is vague and apologetic, offering no specific ask. Option D deflects responsibility rather than requesting a concrete accommodation.

questions.question_text: During an argument, a person feels a surge of anger, says "I'm taking ten," and leaves the room, having agreed on this protocol with their partner in advance. The partner follows them, saying "we're not done — you always run away." Using this chapter's framing, how should this exchange be evaluated?

options.A: The person leaving is doing the skill correctly by buying time for the surge to decay; the partner's pursuit undermines the mechanism, though their need for the conversation to resume afterward is legitimate and should be honored when the pause ends
options.B: Both people handled the moment equally well
options.C: The person leaving is avoiding responsibility and should be required to stay and argue it out
options.D: The partner is right to follow, since walking away from any argument is always harmful

questions.explanation: The chapter's own worked example grades this exact exchange this way: the pre-agreed pause is the skill working and should be praised, while pursuit refuels the surge and punishes the skill — though the conversation must genuinely resume afterward for the protocol to hold trust. Option B ignores that one move helps and the other harms. Option C mislabels a regulation skill as avoidance. Option D overgeneralizes a specific pre-agreed protocol into a universal rule about leaving arguments.

questions.question_text: A person who was recently diagnosed with ADHD finds that nearly every conversation, hobby, and social media feed they engage with now revolves entirely around ADHD content, several months after diagnosis. Using this chapter's analysis of identity after diagnosis and online ADHD culture, what is the best way to understand this pattern?

options.A: This proves the diagnosis must be wrong, since a real diagnosis wouldn't take over someone's whole identity
options.B: This is a permanent and unavoidable state that everyone with ADHD experiences forever
options.C: This likely reflects the common "over-merger" phase, often amplified by algorithmic feeds that reward engagement with ADHD content, and it typically settles over time as the person integrates ADHD as one part of a larger identity
options.D: Online ADHD content is entirely unreliable and should be avoided completely

questions.explanation: The chapter names over-merger as a common, usually temporary phase, and notes that algorithmic feeds amplify it by making ADHD content someone's whole scroll once engagement is detected — it typically settles into ADHD as one part of a larger identity. Option A misreads a common phase as proof against the diagnosis. Option B contradicts the chapter's description of over-merger as usually temporary. Option D overcorrects; the chapter values online community for validation and tactics while cautioning only about medical claims.

questions.question_text: What is active recall?

options.A: Rereading the same material multiple times until it feels familiar
options.B: Listening to a lecture recording at double speed
options.C: Closing the book and retrieving material from memory — flashcards, practice problems, brain dumps — rather than re-reading it
options.D: Highlighting key terms in a textbook with colored markers

questions.explanation: Active recall means closing the book and retrieving material from memory rather than re-reading it, which supplies instant feedback and exposes the illusion that familiarity equals knowledge. Option A describes the passive default the chapter argues against. Option B and D are other passive study habits the chapter doesn't identify as active recall.

questions.question_text: What is the key legal difference between an IEP and a 504 plan?

options.A: A 504 plan provides accommodations that change conditions of access, while an IEP can also include specialized instruction, services, and measurable goals
options.B: An IEP only applies to college students, while a 504 plan only applies to K-12 students
options.C: A 504 plan requires a full team meeting and annual review, while an IEP requires no paperwork at all
options.D: There is no real difference; the two terms describe the same legal document

questions.explanation: The chapter explains a 504 plan changes conditions of access, while an IEP — under IDEA — can also include specialized instruction, services, and measurable annual goals with a heavier process. Option B reverses the actual scope; IEPs end at high school graduation, not college. Option C reverses which document has the heavier process. Option D denies a distinction the chapter treats as central.

questions.question_text: According to this chapter, what is the key structural difference between K-12 accommodations and college disability services?

options.A: College accommodations are automatically identical to whatever plan existed in high school
options.B: Colleges automatically contact parents whenever a student's grades decline
options.C: IEPs continue to apply automatically once a student enters college
options.D: In college, the student must self-identify, provide documentation, and activate accommodations each term — parents are legally outside the process

questions.explanation: The chapter's central structural point is that college disability services activate only when the student self-identifies and provides documentation, with parents legally outside the process under FERPA. Option A is false; college accommodations require new registration, not automatic carryover. Option B contradicts FERPA privacy protections the chapter describes. Option C is directly contradicted; IDEA and IEPs end at high school graduation.

questions.question_text: Why does this chapter describe school accommodations as "the ramp, not a head start"?

options.A: Because accommodations give students an unfair advantage over their peers
options.B: Because accommodations are only available to students with perfect grades
options.C: Because accommodations remove the disability's impact from the measurement, so the material being tested — not the time blindness or working memory limits — is what actually gets assessed
options.D: Because accommodations replace the need to learn the material at all

questions.explanation: The chapter's ramp analogy means accommodations remove the disability's impact from what's being measured, so a chemistry exam tests chemistry rather than time blindness or working memory. Option A treats a leveling measure as an unfair edge, which the chapter explicitly rejects. Option B invents a grade requirement that doesn't exist. Option D wildly overstates what accommodations change.

questions.question_text: Why does this chapter recommend using an app that automatically schedules spaced repetition reviews, rather than relying on remembering to review?

options.A: Because running a review schedule on prospective memory invites the same unreliable-alarm failure this book has described throughout, so a tool that fires on its own is more dependable
options.B: Because apps are required by every school's official curriculum
options.C: Because spaced repetition doesn't actually improve retention
options.D: Because apps guarantee perfect exam scores regardless of study quality

questions.explanation: The chapter is explicit that spaced repetition shouldn't run on prospective memory, since that's an unreliable system, and recommends tools that fire automatically instead. Option B invents a curriculum requirement. Option C contradicts the chapter's endorsement of spaced repetition as high-value. Option D overstates the guarantee any study tool can offer.

questions.question_text: Why does this chapter treat genuine interest as a "structural requirement, not a luxury" when choosing a college major?

options.A: Because interest has no real effect on academic performance
options.B: Because a major that doesn't hold genuine interest will extract a heavy procrastination tax every week, while one that grabs the student can draw on hyperfocus for free
options.C: Because only students without ADHD need to consider interest when choosing a major
options.D: Because interest guarantees a major will lead to a high-paying career

questions.explanation: The chapter argues that the interest-based nervous system makes genuine interest structural: a boring major extracts a weekly procrastination tax, while an interesting one draws on hyperfocus for free. Option A contradicts the chapter's central point about interest and performance. Option C is backwards; interest matters especially for ADHD brains. Option D makes a career-outcome claim the chapter never states.

questions.question_text: A parent wants to request accommodations for their child and is deciding between simply mentioning the diagnosis to the teacher at conferences or sending a formal request. Based on this chapter's playbook, which approach is more likely to succeed?

options.A: Mentioning it casually at conferences, since teachers will remember and act on verbal requests
options.B: Waiting until grades drop significantly before making any request
options.C: Asking the student to explain their own needs to the teacher without any parental involvement
options.D: Putting the request in writing, attaching the evaluation report, and listing specific, mechanism-linked accommodations rather than a general request for help

questions.explanation: The chapter's Amara example contrasts a casual mention that changes nothing with a written request, attached documentation, and specific asks that produce a real, signed plan. Option A is exactly the ineffective approach the chapter's worked example shows failing. Option B delays past the point where the process should start. Option C skips the parent's role in elementary and middle school, where the chapter still expects parental involvement.

questions.question_text: A college student struggles with time blindness during long exams. Which test-taking strategy from this chapter directly addresses this problem?

options.A: Skipping the exam entirely to avoid the anxiety
options.B: Writing a per-section time budget on the exam margin at the start and setting checkpoint questions to track pacing
options.C: Answering questions in a random order with no plan
options.D: Relying on the professor to announce when time is running low

questions.explanation: The chapter specifically recommends writing a time budget in the margin at minute zero and setting checkpoint questions to counter time blindness during a fixed-time exam. Option A avoids the problem rather than addressing it. Option C removes the triage strategy the chapter recommends. Option D outsources time management to someone who isn't obligated to provide it.

questions.question_text: A parent, worried about their college freshman's collapsing grades, calls the dean's office and the student's professors directly to request accommodations on the student's behalf. Based on this chapter's explanation of college disability services, what is the accurate response to this situation?

options.A: This isn't discrimination — post-secondary law makes the student the sole driver of the accommodation process, and FERPA bars the college from discussing the student's situation with a parent regardless of who pays
options.B: The college is required to work with the parent instead of the student, since the parent is paying tuition
options.C: The professors are legally required to grant accommodations immediately upon a parent's request
options.D: This approach is exactly what the chapter recommends parents do to help

questions.explanation: The chapter's own worked example addresses this exact situation: it isn't discrimination, since post-secondary law makes the student the accommodation process's sole driver and FERPA bars the school from discussing the student's situation with a parent. Option B misunderstands FERPA and who tuition payment entitles to information. Option C invents an obligation professors don't have toward a parent's request. Option D contradicts the chapter's explicit guidance that parental help must be indirect at this stage.

questions.question_text: A school tells a family "she's passing all her classes, so she doesn't need a 504 plan," even though the family suspects she is masking significant struggle. Applying this chapter's reasoning together with Chapter 4's concept of high-achievement masking, what is the strongest analysis of the school's position?

options.A: The school is correct; passing grades are the only valid standard for whether accommodations are needed
options.B: Since she is passing, pursuing a 504 plan would be dishonest and should be dropped entirely
options.C: Passing grades can coexist with high private cost from masking, so the disability's impact on access — not the grade outcome — is the legal standard, and the family should ask directly what the grades are costing her
options.D: Masking only affects children who are failing, so it doesn't apply to a student who is passing

questions.explanation: The chapter directly names this failure mode and its counter: passing is not the legal standard, impact on access is, and Chapter 4's masking concept is the evidence that a passing grade can hide serious private cost worth asking about explicitly. Option A accepts the very standard the chapter says is wrong. Option B mistakes advocating for real needs as dishonesty. Option D contradicts the entire premise of high-achievement masking, which specifically describes struggle hidden behind good grades.

questions.question_text: What does "career fit" mean according to this chapter?

options.A: Finding a job listed on a "best careers for ADHD" website
options.B: Choosing the highest-paying job available regardless of daily tasks
options.C: Working exclusively in creative fields, since ADHD only fits creative work
options.D: A role where what the job pays for overlaps with what the person's brain naturally produces, while the "war column" of poor-fit tasks stays small or delegated

questions.explanation: Career fit means a role where the job's paid-for column overlaps with what the person's brain naturally produces, with the difficult "war column" tasks kept small or delegated, illustrated by the nurse who thrived in the ER but struggled in records and compliance. Option A is exactly the internet genre the chapter warns against. Option B ignores daily task fit entirely. Option C wrongly restricts fit to one field, which the chapter never claims.

questions.question_text: In plain language, what does the ADA require of employers regarding ADHD?

options.A: Employers with 15 or more employees must provide reasonable accommodations to qualified employees whose ADHD substantially limits major life activities, through a good-faith interactive process
options.B: Employers must automatically promote any employee who discloses ADHD
options.C: Employers must fire any employee who cannot perform every task without accommodation
options.D: Employers are legally forbidden from ever asking about accommodations

questions.explanation: The chapter explains that ADA-covered employers must provide reasonable accommodations to qualified employees through a good-faith interactive process, while the employee must still perform the job's essential functions. Option B invents an unrelated promotion requirement. Option C contradicts the entire purpose of accommodations, which exist so employees don't need to be fired. Option D misstates the interactive process the ADA actually requires.

questions.question_text: What is "graduated disclosure," as described in this chapter?

options.A: Announcing a diagnosis to the entire company on the first day of a new job
options.B: Never telling anyone at work about an ADHD diagnosis under any circumstances
options.C: Starting with informal, specific asks with no diagnosis attached, then escalating to partial or full formal disclosure only if needed
options.D: A legal requirement to disclose ADHD within the first 90 days of employment

questions.explanation: Graduated disclosure starts with informal, no-diagnosis-attached specific asks, escalating to partial and then formal disclosure only as needed, reserving the ADA's full machinery for when it's actually required. Option A is the opposite of graduated — it's maximal disclosure on day one. Option B forecloses a strategic option the chapter treats as legitimate but not mandatory. Option D invents a legal deadline that doesn't exist.

questions.question_text: Why does this chapter warn against "top 10 careers for ADHD" lists and describe ADHD-friendly work as a shape instead?

options.A: Because no job is ever suitable for someone with ADHD
options.B: Because such lists are always completely accurate and reliable
options.C: Because only medical doctors can determine appropriate careers for people with ADHD
options.D: Because fit depends on structural features like urgency, novelty, visible results, and movement, which can appear in many different jobs and professions, not a fixed list of job titles

questions.explanation: The chapter calls career-list genres "astrology with a salary column" because what actually matters is a shape — urgency, novelty, visible results, movement — that shows up across many different jobs, not a fixed set of titles. Option A contradicts the chapter's entire premise that good fits exist. Option B is the opposite of the chapter's warning. Option C invents an unsupported credentialing requirement.

questions.question_text: According to this chapter, why does remote work sometimes create serious problems for people with ADHD, even though it also offers real benefits?

options.A: Remote work removes the office's built-in structural scaffold — ambient body doubling, physical transitions, and visible social accountability — which must be deliberately rebuilt or the situation resembles the unstructured college cliff
options.B: Remote work is illegal for employees with ADHD
options.C: Remote work always improves ADHD symptoms with no downsides
options.D: Remote work eliminates the need for any accommodations at all

questions.explanation: The chapter's honest two-sided view is that remote work removes the office's ambient structure — other people's presence, physical transitions, visible accountability — and without deliberately rebuilding that scaffold, the result resembles the unstructured college cliff. Option B is a fabricated legal claim. Option C ignores the losses the chapter details alongside the gains. Option D contradicts the chapter's point that structure must be actively rebuilt, not eliminated as a need.

questions.question_text: What does this chapter identify as the central hazard of entrepreneurship for people with ADHD, despite its genuine appeal?

options.A: Entrepreneurship is illegal for people with a disability
options.B: Entrepreneurship never appeals to people with ADHD
options.C: As their own manager, bookkeeper, and compliance department, a founder carries the entire admin tax personally with no institutional scaffolding, unless they deliberately buy or partner for those executive functions
options.D: Founders with ADHD are required to disclose their diagnosis to investors

questions.explanation: The chapter names the hazard plainly: a founder is their own manager, bookkeeper, and compliance department, so the entire admin tax lands unbuffered — the fix is deliberately buying or partnering for those executive functions early. Option A is a fabricated legal claim. Option B directly contradicts the chapter's statement that founders over-index on ADHD traits. Option D invents a disclosure requirement that doesn't exist.

questions.question_text: After a performance review that included one critical comment, an employee feels certain they are about to be fired and can't stop replaying the meeting. Using this chapter's approach to handling feedback at work, what should they do?

options.A: Immediately quit before they can be fired
options.B: Take notes during the meeting as a pause, then later sort the specific items into "fix" versus "feeling," treating the notes as information about work product rather than a verdict on their whole self
options.C: Ignore all future feedback from that manager permanently
options.D: Send an angry email to the manager right after the meeting to defend themselves

questions.explanation: The chapter's kit for handling feedback recommends note-taking as a built-in pause, then sorting items into "fix" versus "feeling" later, holding two readings rather than treating the feedback as a verdict on personhood. Option A is an extreme overreaction the chapter warns against. Option C would prevent legitimate course-correction the chapter values. Option D skips the pause the chapter specifically recommends before any written response.

questions.question_text: An employee has a large project due in six weeks and knows self-imposed personal deadlines rarely hold. Using this chapter's advice on deadlines at work, what should they do?

options.A: Wait until the week before the deadline to start, since nothing else has worked before
options.B: Send the manager a stage plan with specific interim dates, converting the distant deadline into several nearer ones with institutional visibility
options.C: Ask the manager to remove the deadline altogether
options.D: Keep the plan entirely private so no one notices if a stage slips

questions.explanation: The chapter recommends manufacturing institutional witnesses by sending the manager a stage plan with dates, converting one distant deadline into several nearer ones with an audience — which often reads as exceptional professionalism. Option A repeats the pattern the scaffold is designed to prevent. Option C avoids the actual problem rather than solving it. Option D removes the audience effect that makes the stage plan work.

questions.question_text: Newly diagnosed and excited, someone plans to announce their ADHD to their entire team on Monday morning, believing "honesty is the right move." Based on this chapter's distinction between self-acceptance and disclosure, what is the most fitting advice?

options.A: First identify what specific accommodation is actually needed, consider starting with an informal ask with no diagnosis attached, and treat a decision this permanent as worth writing down and holding for a week before acting on it
options.B: Announce it immediately, since any hesitation means shame
options.C: Never disclose ADHD at work under any circumstances, no matter the situation
options.D: Disclosure decisions should always be made by a manager, not the employee

questions.explanation: The chapter's own worked example addresses this exact impulse: separate self-acceptance from strategic disclosure, identify the actual need, consider the informal graduated path first, and treat an irreversible decision made in diagnosis-week enthusiasm as worth writing down and holding before acting. Option B conflates hesitation with shame, which the chapter never claims. Option C forecloses a legitimate option the chapter treats as sometimes the right call. Option D wrongly removes the decision from the person it belongs to.

questions.question_text: A person notices they've said yes to every exciting new project this quarter, are masking exhaustion at the office daily, and have been running on deadline adrenaline for months — but they still feel fine because they aren't tired, just "busy." Using this chapter's burnout prevention framework, what is the most accurate analysis of their situation?

options.A: Since they don't feel tired, there is no real risk of burnout
options.B: Burnout can only happen to people without ADHD, since ADHD brains thrive on stimulation indefinitely
options.C: This combination — overcommitment by enthusiasm, all-day masking, and adrenaline as a sustained operating system — is exactly the ADHD-specific burnout engine this chapter describes, and because burnout announces itself late, feeling fine now doesn't rule out an approaching collapse
options.D: Working on exciting projects can never lead to burnout, regardless of quantity

questions.explanation: The chapter names precisely this combination as the ADHD-specific burnout engine and warns that burnout announces itself late, which is why scheduled recovery and an outside early-warning observer matter more than how someone currently feels. Option A relies on the unreliable internal signal the chapter explicitly warns against. Option B contradicts Chapter 6's burnout mechanics, which apply directly to ADHD. Option D ignores the chapter's point that enthusiasm-driven overcommitment is exactly how burnout builds.

questions.question_text: According to this chapter, what is the central test that distinguishes support from parenting?

options.A: Support is free; parenting always costs money
options.B: Support happens in public; parenting happens in private
options.C: Support is given by parents; parenting is given by anyone else
options.D: Support is what the person asked for; parenting is what you decided they need

questions.explanation: The chapter's central test, worth printing and taping to a refrigerator, is that support is what the person asked for while parenting is what you decided they need — the same act, like setting up a calendar, can be either depending on who initiated it. Option A invents an unrelated financial distinction. Option B and C invent distinctions about location or family role that the chapter never makes.

questions.question_text: What is the mechanical difference between a reminder and a nag, according to this chapter?

options.A: A reminder is requested, specific, and delivered through an agreed channel; a nag is unrequested, repeated, and delivered with rising emotional intensity
options.B: A reminder is always written; a nag is always spoken aloud
options.C: There is no real difference; both terms describe the same behavior
options.D: A reminder comes from a parent; a nag comes from a partner

questions.explanation: The chapter defines the difference mechanically rather than morally: a reminder is requested, specific, and delivered through an agreed channel, while a nag is unrequested, repeated, and rising in emotional charge. Option B invents a format-based distinction the chapter doesn't make. Option C denies a distinction the whole section is built around. Option D invents a relationship-based rule not in the text.

questions.question_text: What four questions does this chapter suggest offering as a menu before providing help?

options.A: Do you want money, time, space, or silence?
options.B: Do you want praise, criticism, advice, or nothing?
options.C: Do you want solutions, company, a reminder system, or just to vent?
options.D: Do you want a doctor, a therapist, a coach, or a friend?

questions.explanation: The chapter's canonical ask-first menu is exactly this: solutions, company, a reminder system, or just to vent — offered explicitly rather than assumed. Options A, B, and D are plausible-sounding but invented menus not found in the chapter's text.

questions.question_text: According to this chapter's description of family system impact, what is the "compensator" role?

options.A: A sibling who develops ADHD symptoms through observation
options.B: A family member, usually a parent or partner, who absorbs the executive load — tracking appointments, forms, and refills — slowly converting from family member into logistics department
options.C: A professional hired to manage the household's finances
options.D: The family member who receives the ADHD diagnosis

questions.explanation: The compensator is the family member, usually a parent or partner, who absorbs the executive load and gradually converts from family member into logistics department. Option A describes an impossible transmission mechanism. Option C invents a professional role the chapter doesn't discuss in this context. Option D confuses the compensator with the person actually diagnosed.

questions.question_text: Why does this chapter recommend dividing household labor by "task shape" rather than a strict 50/50 split by volume?

options.A: Because a 50/50 split is illegal in most households
options.B: Because household labor should always fall entirely on the partner without ADHD
options.C: Because task shape has no real effect on how reliably a task gets done
options.D: Because matching tasks to what each partner's brain actually produces well — recurring calendar-shaped tasks versus burst, urgent tasks — reduces total household failure, as long as the fitted split is renegotiated as genuinely fair

questions.explanation: The chapter recommends dividing by task shape — burst tasks versus recurring calendar-shaped tasks — because it reduces total household failure, provided the fitted split is honestly renegotiated as fair rather than defaulting to whoever "should" do more. Option A invents a legal claim. Option B contradicts the chapter's fairness requirement. Option C denies the entire mechanism the chapter describes.

questions.question_text: Why does this chapter insist that repair after conflict must include a system change, not just an apology or reconciliation?

options.A: Because a repair that ends in reconciliation but no redesign leaves the same collision conditions in place, scheduling the same fight to recur
options.B: Because apologies are meaningless and should never be offered
options.C: Because system changes are required by family therapists in every case
options.D: Because reconciliation always causes more conflict than it resolves

questions.explanation: The chapter's repair sequence ends with closing the loop through a system change, because a repair without redesign leaves the same triggering conditions in place for next month. Option B dismisses apologies, which the chapter treats as a necessary but insufficient step. Option C invents a professional requirement not stated. Option D contradicts the chapter's positive framing of reconciliation as part of repair.

questions.question_text: A father, worried about his adult daughter's incomplete registration renewal, wants to help. Based on this chapter's supporting-without-parenting test, which action counts as support rather than parenting?

options.A: Installing a tracking app on her phone without telling her, "just to help"
options.B: Mentioning the expired sticker once, then asking if she wants a hand, an alarm, or if it's already handled — and accepting her answer either way
options.C: Renewing the registration himself without telling her
options.D: Calling the DMV directly to handle it on her behalf

questions.explanation: This matches the chapter's exact protocol: notice, offer once, ask which kind of help (or none) is wanted, and accept "it's handled" as a real answer. Option A is unrequested surveillance, explicitly named as parenting. Option C and D both act on her behalf without invitation, removing her ownership of the task and its consequences.

questions.question_text: A couple wants to discuss a difficult financial topic. Following this chapter's communication foundations, when and how should they have this conversation?

options.A: At 9:30 pm, right when the topic comes up, however tired either person is
options.B: In the middle of an unrelated argument, to save time
options.C: During a calm, unhurried time such as a walk in daylight, rather than late at night on a drained executive battery
options.D: Only through angry text messages sent in the heat of the moment

questions.explanation: The chapter's communication foundations specifically recommend timing hard conversations for when the executive battery isn't drained — daylight, calm, ideally a walk — rather than late at night. Option A is the exact bad-timing example the chapter warns against. Option B stacks one conflict onto another rather than scheduling deliberately. Option D removes the calm, in-person conditions the chapter treats as essential.

questions.question_text: A mother whose 28-year-old son was recently diagnosed with ADHD notices he seems to have stopped taking his medication and hasn't replied to her last two texts asking about it. Based on this chapter's guidance on adult child autonomy, what is the most appropriate response?

options.A: Offer once, without surveillance, to be a sounding board or specific kind of support if he ever wants it, then respect his answer — reserving direct intervention only for genuine safety concerns like self-harm
options.B: Continue texting him daily about his medication until he responds
options.C: Call his doctor directly to find out what's going on
options.D: Show up unannounced at his home to confront him about the missed doses

questions.explanation: The chapter's own worked example addresses this nearly identical situation: treatment belongs to the adult child, unrequested monitoring is parenting rather than support, and the one exception to respecting autonomy is genuine safety concern, not a treatment choice. Option B continues the unrequested monitoring the chapter names as the actual problem. Option C and D both override his autonomy over his own treatment and privacy.

questions.question_text: A family notices that arguments about the same undone chore keep recurring — a demand arrives at a bad moment, gets ignored, is repeated with rising frustration, triggers a defensive reaction, ends in a blowup, and everyone comes away feeling their same old story was confirmed, only for tension to build again until the next demand. Using this chapter's analysis of the conflict cycle, what is the most effective way to break this pattern?

options.A: The pattern can only be broken by the person with ADHD changing their behavior; the family member has no role in stopping it
options.B: The only solution is to stop discussing the chore entirely and never bring it up again
options.C: The cycle can be interrupted at any point by either person — by timing the demand better, moving the reminder to a system instead of a person, taking a pause during the defensive spike, or simply naming the loop out loud to reset the conversation
options.D: Conflict cycles like this are permanent and cannot be interrupted once they begin

questions.explanation: The chapter's conflict cycle analysis identifies multiple exit points available to either person — timing, system-based reminders, the pause, or simply calling the loop out loud — none of which require waiting for the other person to act first. Option A wrongly assigns all responsibility to one person when the chapter names exits for both. Option B avoids the underlying issue rather than redesigning the interaction. Option D contradicts the chapter's entire point that the loop can be cut at any stage.

questions.chapter: Partners And Caring For The Caregiver
questions.question_text: What is the "partner-parent trap," as described in this chapter?

options.A: A legal requirement that partners must formally adopt caregiving duties
options.B: A financial trap where couples overspend on ADHD treatments
options.C: A parenting technique recommended for raising children with ADHD
options.D: A dynamic where one partner slides into a logistics-manager role while the other is treated like a supervised teenager, eroding desire on both sides

questions.explanation: The partner-parent trap is the dynamic where one partner drifts into logistics-manager and the other into supervised teenager, which research on ADHD-affected couples names as the strongest predictor of relationship misery, since nobody sustains desire for their case manager. Option A invents a legal requirement that doesn't exist. Option B misplaces the trap as financial rather than relational. Option C confuses it with an unrelated parenting technique.

questions.chapter: Partners And Caring For The Caregiver
questions.question_text: Why does this chapter recommend transferring whole domains — including their tracking — rather than just individual tasks when dividing mental load?

options.A: Because tasks are illegal to divide individually under family law
options.B: Because tracking is impossible to transfer between partners under any circumstances
options.C: Because handing someone a task while keeping its tracking gives them an errand, not a real share of the invisible load that causes burnout
options.D: Because domains are always easier to complete than individual tasks

questions.explanation: The chapter is explicit that handing someone a task while keeping its tracking hands them an errand, not a share of the load — real division transfers whole domains, noticing included, such as "you own everything car-shaped." Option A invents a legal claim. Option B contradicts the chapter's entire recommendation, which assumes tracking can and should transfer. Option D makes an unsupported claim about task difficulty.

questions.chapter: Partners And Caring For The Caregiver
questions.question_text: According to this chapter, what is the dangerous final stage in caregiver strain's typical progression, and why is it especially hard to reverse?

options.A: Identity calcification — "I'm the one who holds everything together" — because at that point being needed has become the caregiver's own compensation, so help gets refused
options.B: Tiredness, because it is the mildest and most temporary stage
options.C: Resentment, because it disappears completely once named out loud
options.D: Burnout, because it is identical to ordinary tiredness with no distinguishing features

questions.explanation: The chapter traces strain from tiredness through resentment to identity calcification, where being needed becomes the caregiver's own compensation, making help feel like a threat rather than relief. Option B misidentifies the mildest stage as the dangerous final one. Option C wrongly claims resentment resolves on its own. Option D denies the distinct signature the chapter gives caregiver burnout.

questions.chapter: Partners And Caring For The Caregiver
questions.question_text: Someone in a two-month-old relationship is deciding when to tell their new partner about their ADHD. Based on this chapter's guidance, what is the best timing and approach?

options.A: Disclose in detail on the very first date, before any patterns are visible
options.B: Wait until after the first serious argument caused by an ADHD-related pattern, so there's a clear example to point to
options.C: Disclose early in seriousness, once some patterns have become visible, using a warm mechanism-pattern-ask formula rather than either extreme
options.D: Never disclose, since ADHD is a private matter with no bearing on a relationship

questions.explanation: The chapter recommends disclosing early in seriousness, once patterns are visible enough to attach the explanation to, using the warm mechanism-pattern-ask formula — not on the first date and not after the first fight, when it reads as excuse. Option A shares context-free information too early. Option B repeats the same timing trap Chapter 13 warned about for employers. Option D contradicts the chapter's framing that a serious partner will eventually live inside the condition regardless.

questions.chapter: Partners And Caring For The Caregiver
questions.question_text: A mother realizes she hasn't had an unscheduled afternoon in over a year, thinks about her son mostly in terms of auditing his behavior, and feels irritated whenever someone offers to help. Using this chapter's self-screening tells, what should she recognize and do?

options.A: These are caregiver strain's warning tells, and the recommended move is to protect her own scheduled respite time and treat her own self-care — sleep, her own activities, honest tracking of these tells — as seriously as any other appointment
options.B: Nothing; these feelings are a normal and permanent part of caregiving that cannot be addressed
options.C: She should hide these feelings from everyone, since admitting them would be a betrayal of her son
options.D: She should immediately hand over all caregiving responsibilities to someone else and disengage entirely

questions.explanation: The chapter names these exact signs — no unscheduled time, audit-mode thinking, irritation at offered help — as the strain tells it asks readers to self-screen for, with the remedy being scheduled respite and self-care treated with the same standing as any other appointment. Option B dismisses tells the chapter treats as actionable warnings. Option C encourages hiding feelings the chapter instead wants named. Option D overcorrects into total disengagement, which the chapter doesn't recommend.

questions.chapter: Partners And Caring For The Caregiver
questions.question_text: A couple negotiates a "squall protocol" for their relationship, agreeing in advance that either partner can take a short pause during a heated moment. One evening, the partner with ADHD says "I need ten minutes" and steps outside during an argument. Based on this chapter, what should happen next?

options.A: The other partner should follow immediately and continue the argument to avoid losing momentum
options.B: The pause should be used to end the relationship discussion permanently
options.C: The partner taking the pause should be criticized afterward for walking away
options.D: The pause should be honored as agreed, and the conversation should genuinely resume afterward rather than being treated as avoidance

questions.explanation: The chapter's squall protocol requires the pause to be pre-agreed and the return guaranteed — honoring the pause and genuinely resuming afterward is what makes the protocol trustworthy for both partners. Option A defeats the protocol's purpose by refusing to honor it. Option B misuses the pause as a way to avoid the topic permanently. Option C punishes the exact skill the chapter wants recognized as constructive.

questions.chapter: Partners And Caring For The Caregiver
questions.question_text: A couple attends generic marriage counseling that assumes both partners have typical neurotypical communication patterns, and it doesn't seem to help their recurring conflicts. Using this chapter's analysis, what is the most likely explanation?

options.A: Counseling never works for any couple facing any kind of challenge
options.B: The couple must not actually be trying hard enough in the sessions
options.C: Generic counseling tools often underperform for ADHD-affected couples because they don't account for the mechanism-based dynamics — like the partner-parent trap — that drive the specific conflict pattern; ADHD-informed counseling addresses this directly
options.D: Only medication, never counseling, can help an ADHD-affected relationship

questions.explanation: The chapter is explicit that generic counseling underperforms for ADHD-affected couples the same way generic CBT underperformed in Chapter 8, and recommends seeking counselors who directly address ADHD-specific dynamics. Option A overgeneralizes a specific mismatch into a blanket claim. Option B blames effort rather than fit, which the chapter never does. Option D dismisses counseling entirely, contradicting the chapter's endorsement of ADHD-informed counseling.

questions.chapter: Partners And Caring For The Caregiver
questions.question_text: A family has been reading this book together, but a year later notices old fights have crept back and the systems they built have quietly decayed. Using this chapter's closing analysis, what does this pattern mean, and what is the recommended response?

options.A: It means the systems ran their normal lifecycle into the maintenance stage — decay is normal operation, not proof anything was fake — and the move is to avoid character verdicts, rebuild smaller, and revise the capstone documents with a year of new data
options.B: It means the whole approach failed and the relationship is fundamentally broken
options.C: It means the person with ADHD never really wanted to change
options.D: It means the family should give up on any further documents or systems permanently

questions.explanation: The chapter's final check-yourself question addresses this exact scenario: decay is normal operation, not relapse, and the move is the maintenance habit practiced throughout the book — no character verdicts, rebuild smaller, and revise both capstone documents with fresh data. Option B and C both convert an expected systems event into a verdict on the relationship or the person, which the chapter explicitly rejects. Option D contradicts the chapter's message that renewal, not abandonment, is the plan.

questions.chapter: Partners And Caring For The Caregiver
questions.question_text: A couple has had the same fight about household logistics every month for over a year, and the non-ADHD partner has become the default tracker of nearly every recurring task despite repeated conversations. Weighing this chapter's guidance on when to seek couples counseling, which judgment is best supported?

options.A: Couples counseling is unnecessary as long as the couple still loves each other, regardless of how long a pattern has persisted
options.B: This is exactly the kind of hardened, long-running pattern this chapter identifies as a clear signal to seek ADHD-informed couples counseling, rather than continuing to try the same conversations alone
options.C: The couple should avoid counseling because it would be an admission that the relationship has already failed
options.D: Any pattern lasting less than five years is too minor to justify seeking outside help

questions.explanation: This scenario matches the chapter's stated signal for seeking counseling — a hardened pattern with a monthly fight running for a year — which describes the partner-parent trap needing outside, ADHD-informed help rather than more of the same unaided conversations. Option A dismisses a chronic pattern the chapter treats as a real warning sign. Option C frames help-seeking as failure, which the chapter directly rejects. Option D invents an arbitrary time threshold the chapter never states.

questions.chapter: Partners And Caring For The Caregiver
questions.question_text: A family wants to build a lasting structure that captures both what the person with ADHD needs from supporters and what the family commits to doing (and not doing) to sustain itself over time. Which combination best synthesizes this chapter's guidance into that structure?

options.A: A single verbal conversation, held once, with no written record kept afterward
options.B: A Personal Owner's Manual written by the person with ADHD paired with a Family Support Plan written by the family, both exchanged, dated, and revisited at a scheduled review date as systems inevitably decay
options.C: A single document written entirely by the caregiver on behalf of the person with ADHD, describing what the family will manage for them
options.D: Separate documents that are never shared with each other, kept private to avoid conflict

questions.explanation: The chapter's two capstones are designed exactly this way — one document from each side, exchanged, dated, and revisited at scheduled review points, since everything in the book eventually needs this kind of externalization. Option A skips the externalization the whole book has argued for. Option C recreates the management-not-support pattern the book warns against throughout. Option D removes the exchange that gives the documents their purpose as an alliance.
